name: Classic-Style Test 5
source: Original questions written for LSAT Trainer in the style and difficulty of recent LSATs. Not LSAC material. MIT licensed.

questions.stimulus: Media critic: The Regional Press Council has urged newspapers to stop printing photographs of accident victims without the consent of the victims' families. But several of the council's own members are editors whose papers have printed exactly such photographs in recent years. So the council's recommendation does not deserve to be taken seriously by anyone in the industry.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the media critic's argument is flawed in that the argument
choices: presumes that a recommendation already followed by most newspapers in the region must be a sound one
fails to consider that printing photographs of accident victims might sometimes serve the public interest
treats the past conduct of some of a recommendation's authors as grounds for rejecting the recommendation itself
draws a conclusion about the conduct of all newspapers from the past conduct of only a few editors
confuses the council's authority to recommend a practice with any authority it might have to enforce that practice
questions.explanation: Whether a recommendation is sound has nothing to do with whether the people making it have always followed it; (C) names this tu quoque flaw. (B) is tempting because it raises a point about the merits, but the critic never addresses the merits at all, and considering that point would only help the critic's conclusion. (D) fails because the critic draws no conclusion about all newspapers.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The council's recommendation against printing accident-victim photos without family consent shouldn't be taken seriously.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Some council members edit papers that have printed such photos.

breakdown.analysis: So what if some council members didn't practice what they preach? A recommendation is good or bad on its merits, not on the track record of the people making it. This is the tu quoque flaw, a kind of ad hominem: 'you do it too, so your advice is worthless.' It's a classic; know it. It's like ignoring your doctor's advice to quit smoking because your doctor smokes. We need an answer that says the critic dismisses advice because its givers don't follow it.

choices.note: The critic never says the recommendation is popular or that most papers follow it. Wrong flaw.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Nearly every newspaper in the region already follows the council's guideline, so the guideline must be a wise one.

choices.note: Tempting, because it sounds like a fair point about the merits. But the critic never touches the merits, and this point would only support the critic's side. Failing to consider a point that helps you isn't the flaw here.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Printing such photos causes families pain, so it is never justified (ignoring that a photo might reveal a dangerous road design).

choices.note: CORRECT. That's exactly the move: the editors' own past conduct is used to dismiss what the council recommends. Hypocrisy in the messengers doesn't make the message wrong.
The conclusion is about the council's recommendation, not about all newspapers. No generalization happens.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Three editors I know printed such photos, so every newspaper in the country does it.

choices.note: Enforcement never comes up. The critic doesn't argue that the council can't enforce its advice.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: The council can't punish papers that ignore its guideline, so the guideline must be mistaken.

questions.stimulus: Forester: Many landowners in the Brenna Hills believe that clearing all the dead wood from their woodlots makes the woods healthier. This belief is mistaken. Fallen logs shelter the salamanders and ground beetles that keep pest insects in check, and as the logs rot they return nutrients to the soil. Removing them, then, deprives the remaining trees of both protection and nourishment.
questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the overall conclusion drawn in the forester's argument?
choices: Fallen logs shelter animals that keep pest insects in check.
Clearing all of the dead wood from a woodlot does not make the woods healthier.
Removing fallen logs deprives the remaining trees of both protection and nourishment.
Landowners in the Brenna Hills should leave all the dead wood in their woodlots.
Rotting logs return more nutrients to the soil than any other source does.
questions.explanation: The forester's point is that the landowners' belief is mistaken, which (B) restates: clearing all the dead wood doesn't make the woods healthier. (C) is tempting because it follows 'then,' but it is an intermediate conclusion that supports the rejection of the belief. (D) adds a recommendation the forester never makes.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The belief that clearing all dead wood makes woods healthier is mistaken.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: 1. Fallen logs shelter pest-eating salamanders and beetles; 2. rotting logs feed the soil; 3. so removing them costs trees protection and nourishment.

breakdown.analysis: Ask which statement supports which. The conclusion is the one everything else supports. 'This belief is mistaken' is the main point; the facts about logs explain why, and the 'then' sentence pulls those facts together into a sub-conclusion that in turn supports 'mistaken.' Watch out: the last sentence has a conclusion word, but it's a stepping stone. We need an answer that restates 'the belief is wrong.'

choices.note: This is a premise, one of the reasons the belief is wrong. Premises are never the main conclusion.
CORRECT. 'This belief is mistaken' just means it's false that clearing all the dead wood makes woods healthier. Everything else in the stimulus supports this.

Tempting, because of the word 'then.' But this sentence is an intermediate conclusion: it's the reason the forester gives for calling the belief mistaken. It supports the main point rather than being it.
Too strong, and it adds a recommendation. The forester says clearing everything doesn't help; that's not the same as telling landowners to leave every scrap of dead wood.
Unsupported superlative. The forester says rotting logs return nutrients, not that they're the biggest source.

questions.stimulus: Researchers tracked 400 adults who had just received a hepatitis vaccine. Those who slept at least seven hours a night during the following week had, according to blood tests taken a month later, substantially more antibodies against the virus than did those who slept less. The researchers concluded that getting adequate sleep after vaccination enhances the body's antibody response to the vaccine.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the researchers' argument?
choices: Some participants who slept more than nine hours a night produced fewer antibodies than some who slept exactly seven hours.
The antibodies produced in response to the hepatitis vaccine decline gradually over a period of several years after vaccination.
Most adults report sleeping fewer than seven hours on at least some nights during a typical week.
The participants who slept less were, on average, no older and no less healthy than those who slept more.
Producing antibodies is only one of several ways in which the immune system responds to a vaccine.
questions.explanation: The study shows only a correlation between sleep and antibody levels; older or less healthy people might both sleep less and respond more weakly. (D) rules out those alternative causes, so the sleep difference becomes the more likely explanation. (A) is tempting but compares people within the well-rested group and, if anything, muddies the link.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Adequate sleep after vaccination boosts the antibody response.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: In a study, people who slept 7+ hours in the week after the vaccine made more antibodies than people who slept less.

breakdown.analysis: Is it the sleep, or something about the people who sleep less? Older people and sicker people often sleep worse, and they might make fewer antibodies regardless. That's a correlation dressed up as a cause. We need an answer that rules out a different difference between the two groups.

choices.note: Tempting, because it's about sleep and antibodies. But it compares people inside the well-rested group, and 'some' vs. 'some' tells us almost nothing. If anything it slightly weakens a simple more-sleep-is-better story.
Interesting fact, but not relevant. How long antibodies last says nothing about whether sleep boosted how many were made.
So? How common short sleep is doesn't bear on whether sleep causes a better response.

CORRECT. Age and general health are the obvious rival explanations: older or sicker people tend to sleep less and could also mount a weaker response. If the short sleepers weren't older or sicker, those rivals are gone, and sleep itself becomes the more likely cause.
Irrelevant. The conclusion is only about the antibody response, so other immune responses don't matter.

questions.stimulus:
Ortega: The city should rezone the old rail yard on Fulton Street to allow housing. The neighborhood badly needs new homes, and the yard has sat empty for twenty years.

Kim: The neighborhood certainly needs homes. But the rail yard's soil is soaked with diesel residue, and cleaning it up would cost more than any developer could recover by selling homes there. Rezoning the yard for housing would accomplish nothing; it should remain zoned for industry.
questions.stem: Ortega and Kim disagree over whether
choices: the old Fulton Street rail yard should be rezoned to allow housing
the neighborhood around Fulton Street needs more housing
the soil at the Fulton Street rail yard is contaminated
the rail yard has been empty for twenty years
developers should be required to pay for cleaning up contaminated sites
questions.explanation: Ortega says the yard should be rezoned for housing; Kim says it should stay zoned for industry, so they disagree about (A). (B) is something both affirm, since Kim concedes the neighborhood needs homes. Ortega says nothing about the soil (C), and Kim says nothing about how long the yard has been empty (D).

setup.label: Arguments
setup.text: Ortega: rezone the yard for housing, since homes are needed and the site is empty; Kim: homes are needed, but cleanup costs make housing there pointless, so keep it industrial.

breakdown.analysis: Where do they actually clash? Kim agrees homes are needed, so that's common ground. The clash is the proposal itself: Ortega says rezone, Kim says don't. To disagree, one speaker must say yes and the other no. We need the answer that both speakers take a side on, and opposite sides.

choices.note: CORRECT. Ortega: yes, rezone. Kim: no, keep it industrial. Clear yes vs. no.
Tempting because it's Ortega's main reason. But Kim explicitly agrees ('certainly needs homes'). That's agreement, not disagreement.
Only Kim talks about the soil. Ortega never says whether it's contaminated, so we can't call it a disagreement.
Only Ortega mentions this, and Kim never disputes it.
Neither speaker says who should pay for cleanup. Kim just says it would cost more than a developer could recover.

questions.stimulus: For the past four months the volcano Mount Teral has been erupting mildly, and fine ash has fallen almost daily on the nearby farming village of Ostin, coating roofs and fields. Yet the number of patients seeking treatment for coughing, wheezing, and other breathing problems at Ostin's only clinic has fallen sharply since the eruptions began.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy described above?
choices: Fine volcanic ash can irritate the lungs and throat even of people who have no previous history of breathing problems.
Ostin's clinic is the only medical facility of any kind within a full day's travel of the village.
Since the eruptions began, most of Ostin's residents have been staying with relatives outside the ashfall area.
The ash falling on Ostin consists of particles small enough to remain in the air for several hours.
Several larger towns farther from Mount Teral have also received light falls of ash over the past four months.
questions.explanation: If most residents have left the ash zone, there are far fewer people around to seek treatment at the clinic, so the number of patients can fall even though the ash is harmful. (A) and (D) only deepen the puzzle by making the ash sound worse, and (B) suggests everyone with breathing trouble would still go to that clinic.

setup.label: Paradox
setup.text: Ash has been falling on Ostin daily, but fewer people are visiting the clinic for breathing problems.

breakdown.analysis: How can breathing complaints drop when the air is full of ash? Notice the stimulus counts patients, not the rate among residents. If the people aren't there, they can't show up at the clinic. We need an answer that explains why fewer patients would come in despite the ash.

choices.note: This makes the ash sound more dangerous, so we'd expect more patients. It deepens the paradox.
This makes it even stranger: if it's the only facility nearby, anyone with breathing trouble should be showing up there.
CORRECT. Most residents are gone. Fewer people in the village means fewer patients at the clinic, even if the ash is bad for the people who stayed.
Again, this makes the ash more harmful, since it stays in the air longer. It deepens the puzzle.
Right topic, wrong place. Other towns' ash doesn't explain what's happening at Ostin's clinic.

questions.stimulus: Ralston Hardware sells two brands of interior paint, Corvo and Tenly, at the same price per gallon. A gallon of Corvo covers about 400 square feet of wall with one coat, whereas a gallon of Tenly covers only about 300 square feet. And in independent tests, a single coat of either brand fully hid the old color on most walls. So a Ralston customer who plans to give a large room one coat of paint ______.
questions.stem: Which one of the following most logically completes the argument?
choices: will probably be more satisfied with the look of the finished walls if Corvo is used rather than Tenly
will need two coats of Tenly to hide the old color as well as one coat of Corvo would
is more likely to find Corvo than Tenly in stock in the desired color at a typical Ralston store
would pay about the same total amount for paint whichever of the two brands the customer chose
will generally spend less money on paint for the job by choosing Corvo rather than Tenly
questions.explanation: Same price per gallon, but Corvo covers a third more wall per gallon, and one coat of either usually hides the old color, so the job takes fewer gallons of Corvo and therefore less money (E). (D) is the tempting misreading that ignores coverage, and (B) confuses square feet covered with how well a coat hides the old color, which the tests say is about equal.

setup.label: Facts
setup.text: 1. Corvo and Tenly cost the same per gallon; 2. a gallon of Corvo covers ~400 sq ft, Tenly ~300; 3. one coat of either usually hides the old color; 4. the customer wants one coat on a large room.

breakdown.analysis: This is a fill-in-the-blank, so treat it like a must-be-true: the blank has to follow from the facts. Put facts 1 and 2 together: same price, but Corvo stretches farther. Fact 3 says one coat of either usually does the job, so you don't need extra Corvo to make up for weaker hiding power. A big room means lots of square feet, and fewer gallons at the same price means less money. We need an answer about cost for the job.

choices.note: Satisfaction with the look is about quality and taste. The facts say only that both brands hide the old color equally well in one coat. Unsupported.

Tempting if you misread 'covers 300 square feet' as 'hides less well.' Coverage is how far a gallon goes; the tests say one coat of either brand hides the old color. Nothing calls for a second coat of Tenly.
Stock and color selection never come up. Right store, wrong topic.
Tempting, because the price per gallon is the same. But the total depends on how many gallons you need, and Corvo needs about a quarter fewer gallons for the same wall. This ignores fact 2.

CORRECT. Same price per gallon, more square feet per gallon, and one coat suffices. A large room needs fewer gallons of Corvo, so the job costs less with Corvo. 'Generally' keeps it modest enough to follow.

questions.stimulus: The Larchmont school district wants more of its high school students to join the orchestra. Most students who join the high school orchestra took string lessons in the district's elementary schools, but the district eliminated those lessons last year to save money. So unless the elementary string lessons are restored, membership in the high school orchestra will decline in the coming years.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the argument?
choices: Not all of the students who would have taken the school lessons will take private string lessons instead.
Most students who took elementary string lessons in the district went on to join the high school orchestra.
Restoring the elementary string lessons would cost the district less than recruiting orchestra members in other ways.
No student who did not take elementary string lessons in the district has ever joined the high school orchestra.
Students who took elementary string lessons play more skillfully in high school than students who did not take them.
questions.explanation: The argument assumes that losing the school lessons means losing the training that feeds the orchestra; if every would-be student simply took private lessons instead, the pipeline would be unaffected. (A) states the modest assumption that not all of them will. (B) is tempting but reverses the premise: the argument says most joiners had lessons, not that most lesson-takers joined, and it doesn't need the latter.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Unless elementary string lessons come back, high school orchestra membership will fall.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Most orchestra members took the elementary lessons; the district cut those lessons last year.

breakdown.analysis: Does cutting the school lessons actually mean kids won't learn strings? What if every one of them just signs up for private lessons? Then the orchestra still gets trained players and nothing changes. We need an answer that blocks the 'they'll learn elsewhere' escape. Test by negation.

choices.note: CORRECT. Negate it: all of the students who would have taken the lessons will take private lessons instead. Then the pipeline is intact and there's no reason to expect a decline. The argument falls apart.
choices.negation: All of the students who would have taken the school lessons will take private string lessons instead.

choices.note: Tempting, but it flips the premise. The argument says most joiners had lessons, not that most lesson-takers joined. Negate it: maybe only 30% of lesson-takers joined. Losing the lessons could still shrink the orchestra.
choices.negation: It is not the case that most students who took elementary string lessons went on to join the orchestra.

choices.note: Wrong dimension: cost. The argument predicts a decline; it doesn't compare the price of different fixes. Negation does nothing.
choices.negation: Restoring the lessons would not cost less than recruiting members in other ways.

choices.note: Too strong. The premise says 'most,' so some members might have skipped the lessons. Negate it and the argument is fine.
choices.negation: At least one student who did not take elementary string lessons in the district has joined the high school orchestra.

choices.note: Skill isn't the issue; the argument is about how many students join. Negate it and the membership argument is untouched.
choices.negation: Students who took elementary string lessons do not play more skillfully in high school than students who did not take them.

questions.stimulus: The Vessian oak grows an unusually thick, spongy bark. The tree is native to dry hillsides where wildfires sweep through every few decades, and a thick layer of bark insulates a tree's living tissue from the heat of a passing fire. Some botanists therefore conclude that the Vessian oak's bark is probably an adaptation that protects the tree from fire.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the botanists' argument?
choices: Most wildfires in the Vessian oak's native range burn through the undergrowth on the hillsides without ever reaching the treetops.
Vessian oaks whose bark has been stripped by people are more likely than other Vessian oaks to die in wildfires.
Some tree species that are not native to fire-prone regions also have thick bark that insulates them from heat.
The spongy bark stores rainwater during the wet season and supplies it to the tree through the summer droughts.
Growing thick bark requires a tree to use resources that it could otherwise devote to growing taller or producing more acorns.
questions.explanation: The botanists infer a trait's function from the fact that it would help with fire. (D) offers a different job the spongy bark does, storing water for droughts, which gives another explanation for why the trait evolved. (B) is tempting but strengthens the argument by showing that bark does protect against fire.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The Vessian oak's thick, spongy bark is probably an adaptation for fire protection.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The oak lives where wildfires happen; thick bark insulates against heat.

breakdown.analysis: Just because a trait could help with fire, does that mean that's what it's for? Lots of traits fit more than one story. This is a function guess, and the standard way to weaken one is to give the trait a different job. It's like deciding a dog's thick coat is for protection from thorns when it's really for warmth. We need an answer that offers another explanation for spongy bark.

choices.note: This doesn't touch the bark. If anything, ground fires reaching the trunk would make thick bark more useful, so it leans toward the botanists.
Tempting, because it's about bark and fire. But it shows bark does protect against fire, so it strengthens. Wrong direction.
Wrong group. Other species' bark doesn't tell us why the Vessian oak's bark evolved. Insulating bark existing elsewhere is consistent with the botanists' view.

CORRECT. Now there's a second job for the bark: the 'spongy' part stores water for droughts. That gives a strong alternative explanation for why the oak evolved this trait, so the fire story is less likely to be the reason.
So? Every trait has costs. A cost doesn't say what the benefit is for, and it fits a fire story just as well.

questions.stimulus: A delivery drone may be licensed by the regional aviation office to fly over residential neighborhoods only if it passes the Marsh noise test. The Skylet drone, which several retailers hope to use for home deliveries next year, has four exposed propellers and no sound-dampening shroud of any kind. So the Skylet cannot be licensed to fly over residential neighborhoods.
questions.stem: The conclusion of the argument follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?
choices: Any drone that is equipped with a sound-dampening shroud can pass the Marsh noise test.
No drone that lacks a sound-dampening shroud can pass the Marsh noise test, whatever its other features.
Drones that pass the Marsh noise test rarely draw complaints from residents of the neighborhoods they fly over.
Most drones with exposed propellers fail the Marsh noise test, even when they are flown at high altitudes.
A drone that cannot be licensed to fly over residential neighborhoods will not be used for home deliveries.
questions.explanation: Licensing requires passing the Marsh test, so we need a link showing the Skylet can't pass; (B) says passing requires a shroud, which the Skylet lacks. (A) is the tempting reversal: it says a shroud is enough to pass, which tells us nothing about drones without one. (D) says only 'most,' leaving room for the Skylet to pass.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The Skylet can't be licensed to fly over residential neighborhoods.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Licensed → passes the Marsh noise test; the Skylet has no sound-dampening shroud.

breakdown.analysis: What does a shroud have to do with the Marsh test? Nothing, so far. The rule is: Licensed → Passes Marsh. Contrapositive: not Passes → not Licensed. To show the Skylet can't be licensed, we need it to fail the test. So we need: no shroud → can't pass, which is the same as Passes → has shroud. Then: Skylet has no shroud → can't pass → can't be licensed. We need the shroud to be a necessary condition for passing, not a sufficient one.

choices.note: Tempting, because it links the shroud to the test. But it's backwards: Shroud → Passes. That says nothing about drones without one. The Skylet might pass some other way.
CORRECT. Passes → Shroud. The Skylet has no shroud, so it can't pass, so it can't be licensed. The chain is complete.
Irrelevant. How passing drones do with residents afterward doesn't tell us whether the Skylet can pass.
'Most' isn't 'all.' The Skylet could be one of the exposed-propeller drones that passes, so the conclusion doesn't follow.
This adds a consequence (no home deliveries) after the conclusion. It doesn't help get to the conclusion.

questions.stimulus: Philosopher: Varga defines a robot as any machine that senses its surroundings and acts on what it senses without moment-to-moment human direction. But consider an ordinary household thermostat: it senses the temperature of a room and switches the furnace on or off with no one directing it. Yet no one would call a thermostat a robot.
questions.stem: The philosopher's argument proceeds by
choices: arguing that a proposed definition is too narrow because it excludes some machines that are clearly robots
questioning whether Varga has the technical expertise needed to define a term that engineers use
proposing a more precise definition that avoids the difficulty the argument identifies in Varga's definition
appealing to the judgment of the engineers who actually design, build, and program robots
describing a case that meets all of a proposed definition's conditions but falls outside the category being defined
questions.explanation: The thermostat satisfies Varga's conditions (it senses and acts without human direction) yet isn't a robot, showing the definition is too broad; (E) describes this. (A) is the tempting reversal: the philosopher shows the definition lets in too much, not that it leaves out real robots. (C) fails because no alternative definition is offered.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: (Implicit) Varga's definition of 'robot' is flawed.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: A thermostat senses and acts without human direction, so it fits the definition; but nobody calls a thermostat a robot.

breakdown.analysis: Is the thermostat a robot that the definition leaves out, or a non-robot the definition lets in? It's a non-robot that gets in. That's a counterexample showing the definition is too broad. A definition can fail two ways: too broad (includes things it shouldn't) or too narrow (excludes things it should). We need an answer that describes a case fitting the definition but not the category.

choices.note: Tempting, because it's the right method (a counterexample to a definition) with the direction reversed. A thermostat isn't a robot being shut out; it's a non-robot being let in. That's too broad, not too narrow.
choices.example: Example of this method: Varga says robots must have arms. But a self-driving delivery cart has no arms, and it's clearly a robot.

choices.note: The philosopher never mentions Varga's qualifications. No attack on the person.
choices.example: Example of this method: Varga is a philosopher, not an engineer, so why should we accept her definition of a robot?

choices.note: No new definition appears. The philosopher only shows the old one fails.
choices.example: Example of this method: Varga's definition includes thermostats, so let's define a robot as a machine that senses, acts, and can change its own goals.

choices.note: The appeal is to ordinary usage ('no one would call'), not to engineers or any experts.
choices.example: Example of this method: Robotics engineers don't consider thermostats robots, so Varga's definition is wrong.

choices.note: CORRECT. The thermostat meets both of Varga's conditions, sensing and acting without moment-to-moment direction, yet it isn't a robot. That's a counterexample showing the definition is too broad.

questions.stimulus: When the Harwick supermarket chain cut the price of its own-brand olive oil by 25 percent last spring, it expected sales of the oil to rise substantially. Instead, sales fell over the following months, even though the prices of competing brands at Harwick stores did not change and the oil itself was not altered in any way.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to explain why sales of Harwick's own-brand olive oil fell?
choices: Many shoppers who buy olive oil judge its quality largely by its price.
Before the price cut, Harwick's own-brand olive oil was already the least expensive olive oil sold in its stores.
Olive oil sales at other supermarket chains in the region rose somewhat last spring.
Harwick advertised the price cut prominently in its weekly flyers and on in-store signs.
The price that Harwick paid its suppliers for olive oil rose sharply last year.
questions.explanation: If shoppers read a low price as a sign of low quality, a deep price cut could make the oil look inferior and drive buyers to other brands, explaining the drop (A). (B) is tempting, but already being the cheapest gives no reason why becoming even cheaper would lose sales. (D) deepens the puzzle, since advertising should have helped.

setup.label: Paradox
setup.text: Harwick cut its own-brand olive oil price by 25%, but sales fell, with competitors' prices and the oil itself unchanged.

breakdown.analysis: Why would a cheaper product sell less? The stimulus rules out the easy answers: competitors didn't cut prices, and the oil didn't change. So the explanation must be about how shoppers react to the price itself. Common sense helps: lots of people assume cheap means worse. We need an answer that makes a lower price a reason to buy less.

choices.note: CORRECT. If shoppers use price as a quality signal, a 25% cut makes the oil look worse, so some switch to pricier brands. That explains falling sales without contradicting anything.
Tempting, because it seems to matter that it was already cheapest. But it doesn't explain why getting even cheaper would cost sales. It leaves the puzzle in place.
This makes it stranger: oil was selling well elsewhere, so the fall at Harwick isn't a general market slump.
This deepens the puzzle. More shoppers knew about the lower price, so sales should have risen.
Wrong dimension: Harwick's costs. What Harwick paid suppliers doesn't explain why shoppers bought less.

questions.stimulus: According to company records, 20 percent of the items that Pardoe Outfitters' customers ordered online last year were returned for refunds or exchanges, compared with only 5 percent of the items bought in Pardoe's stores. Clearly, then, Pardoe's returns staff spent more of their time last year processing returns of online orders than processing returns of in-store purchases.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument
choices: presumes that customers who return items are generally dissatisfied with the company's products or service
fails to consider that some of the company's customers shop both online and in its stores
overlooks the possibility that far fewer items were ordered online than were bought in its stores
draws a conclusion about all retailers from data collected about the customers of a single company
takes for granted that items returned to the company cannot be resold at full price
questions.explanation: A higher return rate doesn't mean more returns: if in-store sales vastly outnumber online orders, 5 percent of a large number can exceed 20 percent of a small one, and the staff's time tracks the number of returns. (C) points this out. (B) is tempting but irrelevant, since a customer's shopping both ways doesn't change how many returns of each kind there were.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Returns staff spent more time on online returns than on in-store returns.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: 20% of online items were returned vs. 5% of in-store items.

breakdown.analysis: Does a higher percentage mean a bigger pile of returns? Not if the bases differ. Imagine 1,000 online items (200 returns) and 10,000 in-store items (500 returns). The online rate is four times higher, but the staff handled more in-store returns. Watch the switch from a rate to an absolute amount; it's a classic, know it. We need an answer that says the argument ignores how many items each channel sold.

choices.note: Customer satisfaction never comes up. The argument is about staff time.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Twice as many online items were returned, so our online customers must dislike us.

choices.note: Tempting, because it sounds like a complication. But it doesn't matter who made the purchases; what matters is how many returns of each type there were.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Online shoppers return more items, so the people who shop online must be pickier (ignoring that the same people also shop in the store).

choices.note: CORRECT. Rates don't tell you totals. If in-store sales were much larger, 5% of them could be more returns than 20% of the online orders, and then the staff would spend more time on in-store returns.
The conclusion is only about Pardoe's staff. No generalization to other retailers.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Our online return rate is high, so online shopping causes high return rates everywhere.

choices.note: The argument never assumes anything about reselling. Irrelevant to staff time.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Returns cost us money, since every returned item has to be thrown away.

questions.stimulus: Zoning principle: A variance allowing a new building to exceed the local height limit should be granted whenever the added height will not cast a shadow on any public park and the developer either includes affordable housing units in the building or restores a historic facade on the site.
questions.stem: Which one of the following judgments most closely conforms to the principle stated above?
choices: The Rowan Street tower will include affordable units and restore a historic facade, though its added height will shade a corner of Rowan Park in the late afternoon. So its variance should be granted.
The Parkway hotel's added height will shade no park, and its developer will restore the site's 1890s bank facade, though the hotel will have no housing. So its variance should be granted.
The Delmar office building's added height will not shade any park, but it will include no affordable units and restore no historic facade. So its variance should be denied.
The Linden apartment building will include affordable units, and its developer says the shade its added height casts on Linden Park will be minor. So its variance should be granted.
The Corso building's added height will not shade any park, and its developer has publicly promised to consider including some affordable units. So its variance should be granted.
questions.explanation: The principle requires no shadow on any park plus either affordable units or a restored historic facade; the Parkway hotel meets the shadow condition and the facade half of the 'or,' so (B) conforms. (C) is tempting, but the principle states only when a variance should be granted, so it can never by itself justify a denial. (A) and (D) involve shade on a park, and (E) offers only a promise to consider affordable units.

setup.label: Principle
setup.text: No shadow on any public park AND (affordable units OR restored historic facade) → grant the variance.

setup.label: Application
setup.text: The right answer must grant a variance where 1. the added height shades no park and 2. the developer does at least one of: includes affordable units, restores a historic facade.

breakdown.analysis: What does the principle let you conclude? Only 'grant.' It never says when to deny, so any 'deny' answer is out. For 'grant,' check two things: no park shade at all, and at least one half of the 'or.' Each trap satisfies only part.

choices.note: Both halves of the 'or' are met, but the shadow condition fails: it shades a corner of Rowan Park. 'Any public park' means even a corner counts.
CORRECT. No park shade, and the developer restores a historic facade, which satisfies the 'or' by itself. The missing housing doesn't matter. Grant follows.

Tempting, because this building does fail the 'or.' But the principle only tells you when to grant. Failing its conditions doesn't trigger a denial; the principle is silent. This confuses a sufficient condition with a necessary one.
Affordable units satisfy the 'or,' but the building does shade Linden Park. 'Minor' shade is still shade, and the developer's say-so doesn't change that.
No shade, but a promise to consider affordable units isn't including them, and there's no facade. The 'or' isn't satisfied.

questions.stimulus: Most of the antique clocks in the Hallam Museum's collection were made before 1850, and every clock in the collection that was made before 1850 has a brass movement. Every brass-movement clock in the collection that has been restored keeps accurate time. Yet fewer than half of the clocks in the collection keep accurate time.
questions.stem: If the statements above are true, which one of the following must also be true?
choices: Most of the clocks in the collection that were made before 1850 have not been restored.
Every clock in the collection that keeps accurate time is a brass-movement clock that has been restored.
At least one of the clocks in the collection that keep accurate time was made after 1850.
The collection includes at least one clock that has a brass movement but that has never been restored.
None of the clocks in the collection that were made after 1850 has a brass movement.
questions.explanation: More than half the clocks are pre-1850 and fewer than half keep accurate time, so at least one pre-1850 clock doesn't keep time; it has a brass movement, and a restored brass clock would keep time, so it is an unrestored brass clock (D). (A) is the dominant trap: the numbers guarantee one unrestored clock, not most. (B) reverses the restored-brass conditional.

setup.label: Facts
setup.text: 1. Most clocks in the collection were made before 1850; 2. made before 1850 → brass movement; 3. brass movement AND restored → keeps accurate time; 4. fewer than half the clocks keep accurate time.

breakdown.analysis: Hard to prephrase, so do the counting. Say there are 100 clocks. More than 50 were made before 1850, but fewer than 50 keep accurate time. So at least one pre-1850 clock does NOT keep accurate time. That clock has a brass movement (fact 2). Contrapositive of fact 3: not accurate → NOT (brass AND restored). It is brass, so it hasn't been restored. That's all the numbers guarantee: ONE such clock, not most. Most students pick (A), because 'most were made before 1850' plus 'fewer than half keep time' feels like it should give 'most pre-1850 clocks are unrestored.' It doesn't: 60 pre-1850 clocks with 45 of them restored (and accurate) fits every fact, and then most pre-1850 clocks ARE restored. 'Some' is not 'most.' The right answer also hides: it never mentions 1850, so it looks off topic until you trace the chain.

choices.note: Tempting. It's the right idea at the wrong strength. Try 100 clocks: 60 made before 1850, 45 of those restored and accurate, 15 not. Fewer than half keep time, yet most pre-1850 clocks are restored. The facts force one unrestored clock, not most.
This reverses fact 3. Restored brass clocks keep accurate time, but nothing says they're the only clocks that do. A clock with some other movement could keep accurate time too.
We don't know this. Every accurate clock could have been made before 1850; nothing requires a later clock to keep time.

CORRECT. Some pre-1850 clock must fail to keep accurate time, since more than half the clocks are pre-1850 and fewer than half keep time. That clock has a brass movement, and a restored brass clock would keep time, so it has never been restored.
We don't know this. The facts say every pre-1850 clock is brass; they say nothing about later clocks, which could have brass movements too.

questions.stimulus: Biographer: While researching my biography of the late composer Edda Varn, I found letters revealing that her younger brother had spent two years in prison for fraud. I will not mention this in the book. The brother's imprisonment had no bearing on Varn's music or career, and making it public would cause considerable distress to his children, who are still living.
questions.stem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the biographer's decision?
choices: A biographer should leave out facts about the subject's relatives that are irrelevant to the subject's work and would greatly distress living people.
A biographer should include any information about the subject's family that is accurate and that was obtained from reliable documents such as letters.
Information that sheds light on a subject's work should always be included in a biography, regardless of the distress it may cause.
A biographer should not quote from private letters unless the writer of the letters has given permission for them to be published.
Whether to include a fact in a biography should depend solely on how much interest the book's readers would be likely to have in it.
questions.explanation: The biographer gives two reasons, irrelevance to Varn's work and serious distress to living people, and (A) says that when both hold, the fact should be left out, which is exactly the decision. (D) is tempting, but the biographer isn't quoting the letters and never relies on permission. (C) covers information that sheds light on the subject's work, which this fact doesn't.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The biography won't mention the brother's prison term.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The imprisonment had no bearing on Varn's music or career; making it public would greatly distress the brother's living children.

breakdown.analysis: What rule turns those two reasons into 'leave it out'? A principle-justify answer has to tell you to do what the conclusion says, using the facts you've got. Here: irrelevant to the subject's work + causes distress to living people → omit. We need a principle with exactly that shape.

choices.note: CORRECT. Both conditions are met: the brother's prison term is irrelevant to Varn's work, and publishing it would greatly distress his living children. The principle then says leave it out, which is the biographer's decision.
This points the other way. The letters are reliable documents and the fact is presumably accurate, so this principle says include it.
This covers facts that shed light on the subject's work. The biographer says this one doesn't, so the principle doesn't apply and can't justify the decision.

Tempting, because it's about the letters and it would block something. But the biographer isn't planning to quote the letters, and the stated reasons are relevance and distress, not permission. Even if it applied, it would only stop quotation, not mention of the fact.
Wrong dimension: reader interest. Readers might be very curious about a family scandal, which would push toward including it. It doesn't support the decision.

questions.stimulus: Consumer reporter: Each year our magazine prices the same basket of groceries at the twelve largest supermarkets in the county. Two years ago, Valdane Foods had the cheapest basket of the twelve; this year it ranked only fifth. So shoppers who have stayed loyal to Valdane are now paying more for their groceries than they were two years ago.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the consumer reporter's argument is flawed in that the argument
choices: presumes that Valdane's loyal shoppers choose where to shop solely on the basis of the prices that stores charge
takes for granted that the magazine collected and priced the basket of groceries in the same way in both years
overlooks the possibility that Valdane dropped to fifth place because several of the other eleven supermarkets lowered their prices
fails to consider that the four supermarkets now ranked above Valdane may have raised their prices by less than Valdane did
fails to consider that shoppers who stopped going to Valdane may now be paying even more at other nearby supermarkets
questions.explanation: A ranking is relative: Valdane can fall from first to fifth while its own prices stay flat, if other stores cut theirs, which is the possibility (C) says the reporter overlooks. (D) is the dominant trap: it sounds like the relative-ranking point, but rivals raising prices by less than Valdane did concedes that Valdane raised its prices, which fits the conclusion. (B) questions something the stimulus already grants: the same basket is priced each year.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Loyal Valdane shoppers pay more for groceries now than two years ago.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Valdane went from cheapest of twelve to fifth cheapest in the magazine's basket comparison.

breakdown.analysis: Does falling in a ranking mean your number went up? No. Rankings are relative. If you run the same time in a race but four people speed up, you drop to fifth without getting any slower. Valdane's prices might be unchanged, or even lower. This is the ranking-to-absolute shift: watch for it whenever a conclusion about 'more' or 'less' comes from a rank. We need an answer that says other stores' changes could explain the drop. Most students pick (D), because it talks about the other stores' prices, just as the right answer does. But (D) says those stores raised prices by LESS than Valdane did, which means Valdane did raise its prices. That agrees with the conclusion, so it can't be what the argument gets wrong.

choices.note: The argument isn't about why shoppers pick stores; it's about what loyal shoppers pay. Nothing here assumes price is their only reason.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Valdane is no longer the cheapest, so its loyal shoppers will surely leave for a cheaper store.

choices.note: The stimulus already says the magazine prices the same basket each year, so this questions a premise rather than the reasoning. And even with an identical method, a drop in rank wouldn't show that Valdane's prices rose.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Our survey found Valdane cheapest two years ago and fifth this year, so prices there must have risen (when this year's survey used a different basket).

choices.note: CORRECT. If several rivals lowered their prices, Valdane could slide to fifth while charging exactly what it did before. Then its loyal shoppers aren't paying more at all. The argument treats a drop in rank as a rise in price.

Tempting, because it's about how the other stores' prices moved, which is where the real flaw lives. But 'raised their prices by less than Valdane did' means Valdane raised its prices. That's the reporter's conclusion. A possibility that agrees with the conclusion can't be what the argument overlooks.
Wrong group. The conclusion is about shoppers who stayed loyal, not those who left.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Former Valdane shoppers pay more now, so loyal Valdane shoppers must pay more too.

questions.stimulus: Council member: Three years ago, the city rezoned the Harbor Street corridor to forbid any new building taller than four stories. Not a single new office building has been built along the corridor in the three years since then, though several went up there in the decade before. Clearly, the rezoning has discouraged office development there.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption on which the council member's argument depends?
choices: Most developers who build office buildings in the city prefer to build ones that are taller than four stories.
Had taller buildings still been allowed on the corridor, at least one new office building would probably have gone up there.
No new residential buildings of any height have been built along the Harbor Street corridor since the rezoning either.
The rezoning was adopted chiefly in order to discourage further office development along the Harbor Street corridor.
Demand for office space in the city as a whole has not declined at all over the past three years.
questions.explanation: Blaming the rezoning for the absence of office buildings requires that, without it, some office building would probably have gone up; (B) says this, describing the counterfactual as taller buildings still being allowed. (E) is the dominant trap: ruling out a fall in demand sounds like the needed defender, but 'not declined at all' is far stronger than the argument needs, since a slight dip is compatible with the rezoning's having discouraged development. (A) is also too strong.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The rezoning discouraged office development on the corridor.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: A four-story limit was imposed three years ago; no new office buildings have been built since.

breakdown.analysis: Would anyone have built an office there anyway? If not, then zero new buildings is exactly what you'd expect with or without the rezoning, and the rezoning gets no blame. Any time an argument blames an action for an outcome, it assumes the outcome wouldn't have happened without that action. Think of a defense lawyer: 'It would have happened anyway.' We need the answer that shuts that defense down. Here it hides: it never says 'rezoning,' only 'had taller buildings still been allowed,' which means the same thing. Most students pick (E), because a slump in demand is the obvious alternative cause. But (E) says demand hasn't declined AT ALL. Negate it: demand dipped slightly. The rezoning could still be what stopped construction, so the argument survives. Too strong. Test every choice by negation.

choices.note: Too strong. Negate it: maybe only some developers prefer taller buildings. The rezoning could still discourage those developers, so the argument survives.
choices.negation: It is not the case that most developers who build office buildings in the city prefer to build ones taller than four stories.

choices.note: CORRECT. Negate it: even with taller buildings allowed, probably no office building would have gone up. Then the empty corridor says nothing about the rezoning, and the argument collapses. 'Had taller buildings still been allowed' is just another way of saying 'without the rezoning.'
choices.negation: Even had taller buildings still been allowed on the corridor, probably no new office building would have gone up there.

choices.note: Irrelevant. Residential construction tells us nothing required about office development. Negate it (some homes were built) and the office argument is unaffected.
choices.negation: At least one new residential building has been built along the corridor since the rezoning.

choices.note: Irrelevant. What the council intended doesn't matter; the question is what the rezoning actually did. Negate it (the rezoning was adopted mainly to protect views, say) and it could still have discouraged office building.
choices.negation: The rezoning was not adopted chiefly in order to discourage further office development along the corridor.

choices.note: Tempting, because a slump in demand is the obvious rival explanation. But 'not declined at all' is far too strong. Negate it: demand dipped slightly. A small dip could leave plenty of demand for a new building, so the rezoning could still be the reason none went up. The argument survives.
choices.negation: Demand for office space in the city as a whole has declined at least somewhat over the past three years.

questions.stimulus: In a survey conducted on the trails of the Ondine Hill nature reserve last month, 85 percent of the visitors interviewed said they support banning dogs from the reserve's trails. The reserve's managers concluded that a large majority of the reserve's regular users would favor such a ban, and they plan to adopt it next spring.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the managers' argument?
choices: Dogs that are allowed on trails sometimes disturb nesting birds and other wildlife that live in nature reserves.
Some of the visitors who said they support the ban had recently been bothered by an unleashed dog on the trails.
Several nearby parks that already ban dogs from their trails have seen no drop in the number of their visitors.
Visitors were interviewed only if they agreed to stop and answer questions, and a few of them declined.
Last month, trail repairs had temporarily closed the reserve to dogs, so few dog owners visited it.
questions.explanation: The managers generalize from last month's visitors to the reserve's regular users; (E) shows the sample left out the very people most likely to oppose the ban, dog owners, so the 85 percent figure likely overstates support. (D) is tempting, but a few refusals give no reason to think those who declined differed in their views. (A) and (C) bear on whether a ban is wise, not on what users think.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: A large majority of the reserve's regular users would favor a ban on dogs on the trails.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: 85% of visitors interviewed on the trails last month said they support the ban.

breakdown.analysis: Who got asked? Visitors on the trails last month. Are they like the reserve's regular users? If some regulars were missing from that month, the survey could badly misjudge them. The group with the most at stake is dog owners. We need an answer showing the sample left out people whose views would differ, especially dog owners. This is a sampling flaw; it's a classic, know it.

choices.note: Interesting fact, but not relevant. It's a reason a ban might be wise, not evidence about what the reserve's users think.
So? This explains why some supporters feel the way they do. It doesn't suggest the people surveyed were unlike the reserve's regular users.
Wrong dimension. Whether bans hurt attendance elsewhere says nothing about whether this reserve's users favor one.
Tempting, because non-response can bias a survey. But only a few declined, and nothing suggests they held different views. Possible bias isn't shown bias.

CORRECT. Dogs were barred last month, so dog owners mostly stayed away, and they're the users most likely to oppose a ban. The sample is skewed toward supporters, so 85% probably overstates support among regular users.

questions.stimulus: Over the past decade, the lichens that once covered the old stone walls of the Durrow churchyard have almost entirely disappeared. Botanists attribute the loss to exhaust from the bypass road that opened beside the churchyard eleven years ago. Lichens have no roots and draw water and nutrients directly from the air, so they take in whatever pollutants the air carries.
questions.stem: Each of the following, if true, strengthens the botanists' argument EXCEPT:
choices: Because lichens grow extremely slowly, a wall that has lost its lichens may take decades to be fully recolonized.
Lichens on the walls of a churchyard five miles from any major road have not declined over the same period.
The walls nearest the bypass road lost their lichens first, and those farthest from the road lost theirs last.
The lichen species that grew on the churchyard walls are known to be unusually sensitive to compounds in vehicle exhaust.
The churchyard walls have not been cleaned, repaired, or treated with any chemicals at any time during the past decade.
questions.explanation: Four choices support the exhaust explanation: a comparison site without a road (B), a decline that tracks distance from the road (C), a mechanism (D), and the ruling out of cleaning or chemicals as rival causes (E). (A) explains why the lichens haven't come back, which fits any cause of the loss equally well, so it doesn't strengthen the claim that exhaust caused it.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Exhaust from the bypass road caused the lichens on the churchyard walls to disappear.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The lichens vanished over the decade after the road opened; lichens absorb whatever pollutants the air carries.

breakdown.analysis: This is a causal claim built on timing plus a plausible mechanism. In an EXCEPT question, four answers strengthen and the right answer doesn't: it can weaken or, more often, just be irrelevant. Prephrase the usual strengtheners: a control site without the road, a dose-response pattern, a known mechanism, and ruling out other causes. Cross off each one you find. The survivor is the answer.

choices.note: CORRECT. This explains why the walls are still bare, but slow regrowth follows any cause of the loss, whether exhaust, cleaning, or disease. It does nothing to point to the road. Tempting to skip because it's about lichen biology and sounds scientific.
Strengthens. It's a control group: similar walls far from a road kept their lichens, so a region-wide cause like weather becomes less likely.
Strengthens. A dose-response pattern: the closer to the exhaust, the sooner the loss. That's what you'd expect if the road is the cause.
Strengthens. It supplies the mechanism: these particular lichens are especially vulnerable to what the road puts into the air.
Strengthens. It rules out obvious rival causes, like scrubbing the walls or treating them with chemicals, that could also strip lichens.

questions.stimulus: Lexicographer: The proposal that the Vellish national dictionary admit a new word only after it has appeared in print in at least three major newspapers should be rejected. Many regional farming and fishing terms, though widely spoken for generations, seldom appear in newspapers. Thus the proposed rule would keep out a good many words in active use. And recording the language as it is actually used is a dictionary's chief purpose.
questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the role played in the lexicographer's argument by the claim that the proposed rule would keep out a good many words in active use?
choices: It is the argument's overall conclusion, which is supported in part by the claim that recording actual usage is a dictionary's chief purpose.
It is a premise that is offered in support of the claim that recording the language as it is actually used is a dictionary's chief purpose.
It is a subsidiary conclusion that is offered in support of the claim that many regional farming and fishing terms seldom appear in newspapers.
It is a conclusion drawn from one claim in the argument and then offered, along with another claim, in support of the overall conclusion.
It is an illustration offered to show that regional farming and fishing terms are seldom printed in major newspapers.
questions.explanation: The overall conclusion comes first: the proposal should be rejected. The farming-and-fishing claim supports 'the rule would keep out many words in active use,' which, together with the claim about a dictionary's purpose, supports rejecting the proposal (D). (A) is the dominant trap set by 'Thus': the claim is a conclusion, but only an intermediate one. (C) gets the role right but runs the support the wrong way.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The three-newspapers proposal should be rejected.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: 1. Many widely spoken regional terms seldom appear in newspapers; 2. so the rule would keep out many words in active use; 3. a dictionary's chief purpose is to record actual usage.

breakdown.analysis: Ask which statement supports which. The conclusion is the one everything else supports, and here it sits in the first sentence with no indicator word. The structure is: regional terms seldom printed → rule keeps out words in active use; that claim + 'a dictionary records actual usage' → reject the proposal. The 'Thus' marks a stepping stone, not the main point. So the claim in the stem is supported (by the farming-and-fishing claim) and supports (the rejection, alongside the purpose claim). We need an answer that captures both directions. Most students pick (A), because 'Thus' is the loudest conclusion signal in the passage. It fails because the claim is itself offered as a reason to reject the proposal, so it can't be the overall conclusion. And watch (C): it uses the right label, 'subsidiary conclusion,' but points the arrow the wrong way. Most students pick (A), because 'Thus' is the loudest conclusion signal in the passage. It fails because the claim is itself offered as a reason to reject the proposal, so it can't be the overall conclusion. And watch (C): it uses the right label, 'subsidiary conclusion,' but points the arrow the wrong way.

choices.note: Tempting, because 'Thus' flags it as a conclusion. But it's not the overall one: the argument's point is that the proposal should be rejected, and this claim is a reason for that. Also, the purpose claim doesn't support it; the two work side by side.
Wrong relation. The claim about a dictionary's purpose is a standalone premise; nothing in the argument is offered to support it.

Right label, wrong direction. It is a subsidiary conclusion, but it is supported BY the claim about farming and fishing terms; it isn't offered in support of that claim. Right role, wrong relation is a common Role trap.

CORRECT. It's drawn from the claim about regional terms ('Thus'), and it works with the claim about a dictionary's chief purpose to support rejecting the proposal. Abstract wording, but every piece checks out.
This reverses the support. The claim about regional terms supports the claim in the stem, not the other way around.

questions.stimulus: Columnist: Advocates of Corvex lozenges claim that the lozenges shorten the common cold. Their only evidence is a trial in which people who took the lozenges recovered faster than people who did not. But in that trial, the people given the lozenges were also told to drink extra fluids, and the others were not. So Corvex lozenges do not shorten the common cold.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the columnist's argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument
choices: fails to consider that the advocates may have further evidence that the lozenges shorten colds
presumes that the results of a single trial must hold for everyone who catches a cold
attacks the motives of the lozenges' advocates rather than addressing the evidence they offer for their claim
overlooks the possibility that the lozenges shorten colds even though the trial does not show it
takes for granted that drinking extra fluids is what actually shortened the colds of the people given lozenges
questions.explanation: The columnist shows only that the trial can't separate the lozenges' effect from the fluids' effect. That leaves the advocates' claim unproven, not disproven, and (D) names the possibility the columnist ignores: the lozenges might work anyway. (E) is the dominant trap: the columnist needs only that fluids might have shortened the colds, not that they did. (A) is ruled out by the stimulus, which says the trial is their only evidence.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Corvex lozenges don't shorten colds.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The advocates' only evidence is a trial in which the lozenge group was also told to drink extra fluids.

breakdown.analysis: So the trial was confounded. Does that prove the lozenges don't work? No. It proves the trial doesn't show that they do. Knocking out someone's evidence leaves their claim unsupported, not false. It's like saying: my friend's proof that it will rain tomorrow was bad, so it won't rain. Rebutting an argument isn't the same as disproving its conclusion; it's a classic, know it. We need an answer that says the lozenges could still work even though the trial doesn't show it. Here it's written as an omission ('overlooks the possibility that…'), not the textbook 'treats lack of proof as disproof,' so it's easy to read past. Most students pick (E), because the fluids are the columnist's whole point. But the columnist never needs fluids to be the real cause; showing that they MIGHT be is enough to make the trial inconclusive.

choices.note: Tempting, since overlooking other evidence is a common flaw. But the stimulus says the trial is the advocates' only evidence, so there's nothing the columnist overlooked.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: The one study I read on this vitamin found no effect, so no evidence for the vitamin exists.

choices.note: This describes what the advocates might do, not what the columnist does. The columnist doesn't generalize from the trial at all.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Lozenges helped the people in one trial, so they'll help everyone who catches a cold.

choices.note: The columnist addresses the evidence directly and never mentions motives.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: The lozenge advocates are paid by Corvex, so their claims can be ignored.

choices.note: CORRECT. The trial is confounded, so it doesn't show the lozenges work, but they could still work. The columnist concludes they don't, which needs much more than a flawed trial. That possibility is exactly what the argument overlooks.

Tempting, because the fluids are the columnist's whole point. But the rebuttal only needs fluids to be a possible cause; that's enough to make the trial inconclusive. The columnist doesn't need to assume fluids actually work.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: The lozenge group recovered faster, and they drank extra fluids, so fluids are what cured them.

questions.stimulus: The cleaning robots in the Ferro warehouse are programmed never to drive onto any area of floor that their shared map marks as wet, and they have never been known to disobey this programming. The map marks an area as wet whenever the cleaning crew reports having mopped it. Yesterday, one of the robots drove onto a wet area of floor and slipped.
questions.stem: The statements above, if true, most strongly support which one of the following?
choices: Yesterday, the cleaning crew mopped at least one area of floor without reporting that it had done so.
Yesterday, some area of the warehouse floor became wet for some reason other than the crew's mopping.
The robots' map sometimes continues to mark areas of the floor as wet after they have completely dried.
The robots cannot sense whether an area of floor is wet except by consulting their shared map.
Yesterday, not every area of the warehouse floor that the robots' map left unmarked was actually dry.
questions.explanation: Robots never drive onto areas the map marks as wet, yet one drove onto a wet area, so that wet area was unmarked: not every unmarked area was dry (E). (A) is the dominant trap: an unreported mopping is one way the map could have missed the water, but a leak or spill would do just as well, so the facts don't favor it. (B) has the same problem in reverse, and (D) is unsupported.

setup.label: Facts
setup.text: 1. Robots never drive onto areas the map marks as wet (and have never been known to disobey); 2. crew reports mopping an area → the map marks it wet; 3. yesterday a robot drove onto a wet area and slipped.

breakdown.analysis: Hard to prephrase, so link the facts. Robots never drive onto areas marked wet. A robot drove onto a wet area. So that area wasn't marked wet: the map left at least one wet area unmarked. That's all we know. We don't know WHY it was unmarked. Fact 2 is Reported → Marked, a sufficient condition; it doesn't say mopping is the only way floors get wet. Most students pick (A), because an unreported mopping is the first explanation that comes to mind. But a leak, a spill, or a tracked-in puddle would explain it just as well, and nothing says the crew mopped yesterday at all. You can't pick an answer on a possibility. The right answer is a double negative ('not every unmarked area was dry'); translate it: some unmarked area was wet.

choices.note: Tempting. It's one way the map could have missed the wet area. But the water could have come from a leak or a spill, and nothing says the crew mopped yesterday. Possible isn't supported.
The mirror image of (A): another possible cause, equally unsupported. The area might have been mopped and simply not reported.
Wrong direction. The facts show the map missed a wet area, not that it marked a dry one. Nothing here is about stale markings.
We don't know this. The robots might sense wetness perfectly well and still be programmed to follow only the map. A slip doesn't show they can't sense water.
CORRECT. The robot drove onto a wet area, and robots never drive onto areas marked wet, so that wet area was unmarked. 'Not every unmarked area was dry' says exactly that.

questions.stimulus: Every tree that was removed from the Wexley greenbelt this year had been inspected beforehand by the county arborist, who checks trees for disease and storm damage. The old elm by the footbridge, which many residents had feared would be cut down, was not removed this year, so the arborist must not have inspected it.
questions.stem: The flawed pattern of reasoning in which one of the following arguments is most similar to that in the argument above?
choices: Every player who scored a goal for the Hawks this season attended every one of the team's practices. Dev did not attend every practice, so he did not score a goal for the Hawks this season.

Only paintings that had been appraised beforehand by the auction house's experts were sold at the Corvin auction last week. The Varn landscape went unsold at the auction, so no one appraised it beforehand.

Only employees who had completed the company's safety training were assigned to the night shift last month. Rosa was assigned to the night shift last month, so she must have completed safety training.
Every apartment at Elm Court that was repainted this year was also inspected by the building manager. Unit 4 was inspected by the manager this year, so it was probably repainted as well.
Every dish on the café's menu that contains nuts is marked with a small star. The lentil soup on today's menu is marked with a star, so it must contain nuts.
questions.explanation: The argument has the form 'every R was I; X was not R; so X was not I,' which wrongly negates a conditional. (B) has the same form in disguise: 'only appraised paintings were sold' means every sold painting was appraised, and it then infers 'not appraised' from 'not sold.' (A) is the dominant trap because it looks nearly identical on the surface, but it validly uses the contrapositive (not I, so not R); (E) and (D) commit a different flaw, inferring R from I.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The arborist didn't inspect the elm.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Every tree removed this year was inspected first; the elm wasn't removed.

setup.label: Pattern
setup.text: All R are I; X is not R; so X is not I. (Removed → Inspected; not Removed; therefore not Inspected.)

breakdown.analysis: Can a tree be inspected and then left standing? Of course. Inspection might have found it healthy. Removed → Inspected only tells you about removed trees; it says nothing about trees that stayed. Concluding not-Inspected from not-Removed negates the rule without flipping it, a classic error. The only valid move is the contrapositive: not Inspected → not Removed. Translate each choice into arrows and look for: A → B; not A; so not B. Beware: 'Only B are A' means A → B, so the matching answer may be written with 'only.' Most students pick (A), because it copies the stimulus's wording almost exactly. It fails because it runs the valid contrapositive (not I, so not R), and a valid argument can't match a flawed one. The right answer hides behind 'only,' which you must translate before you can see the match. Most students pick (A), because it copies the stimulus's wording almost exactly. It fails because it runs the valid contrapositive (not I, so not R), and a valid argument can't match a flawed one. The right answer hides behind 'only,' which you must translate before you can see the match.

choices.note: Tempting, because the wording looks almost identical to the stimulus. But map it: Scored → Attended every practice; Dev didn't attend; so he didn't score. That's 'not B, so not A,' the valid contrapositive. The stimulus is flawed; this one isn't.

CORRECT. 'Only appraised paintings were sold' means Sold → Appraised. The landscape wasn't sold, so it wasn't appraised: not A → not B. Same flaw as the stimulus, just dressed up with 'only.' An unsold painting could easily have been appraised and then failed to find a buyer.
'Only trained employees were assigned' means Night shift → Trained. Rosa was on the night shift, so she was trained. That's valid: a straight application of the rule.
Repainted → Inspected; Unit 4 inspected; so probably repainted. That's B → A again (affirming the consequent), softened with 'probably.' Different flaw.
Nuts → Star; soup has a star; so nuts. That's B → A, affirming the consequent. A flaw, but a different one from the stimulus.

questions.stimulus: Immunologist: Only vaccines that contain no live virus can safely be given to patients whose immune systems are suppressed, and every patient who has received an organ transplant within the past year has a suppressed immune system. It follows that the newly approved Velmar vaccine, which will be offered at clinics throughout the region this winter, contains no live virus.
questions.stem: The immunologist's conclusion follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?
choices: Any vaccine that contains no live virus can safely be given to patients whose immune systems are suppressed for any reason.
Most patients whose immune systems are suppressed have received an organ transplant at some point within the past year.
The Velmar vaccine can safely be given to at least some patients whose immune systems are not suppressed.
No vaccine that contains live virus has ever been approved for use in patients who recently received organ transplants.
The Velmar vaccine can safely be given to some patients who received an organ transplant within the past year.
questions.explanation: The premises chain: recent transplant → suppressed immune system, and safe for a suppressed patient → no live virus; (E) gives the missing start of the chain, that Velmar is safe for some recent transplant patient, which forces 'no live virus.' (A) is the tempting reversal (no live virus → safe), which says nothing about Velmar. (D) is attractive, but nothing says Velmar was approved for transplant patients.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Velmar contains no live virus.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Safe for a suppressed patient → no live virus; recent transplant → suppressed.

breakdown.analysis: Where does Velmar enter the chain? Nowhere: the premises never mention it. Lay it out: Recent transplant → Suppressed; Safe for a suppressed patient → No live virus. Chain: Safe for a recent transplant patient → (that patient is suppressed) → No live virus. So we need Velmar to be safe for at least one recent transplant patient. Warning: 'Only no-live-virus vaccines are safe' means Safe → No live virus, not the reverse. Most students pick (A), because it links 'no live virus' and 'safe' in the stimulus's own vocabulary. It fails because it reverses the 'only' rule and still never mentions Velmar. The right answer hides, too: it talks about transplant patients rather than suppressed ones, so you have to run the second premise to see that it connects. Most students pick (A), because it links 'no live virus' and 'safe' in the stimulus's own vocabulary. It fails because it reverses the 'only' rule and still never mentions Velmar. The right answer hides, too: it talks about transplant patients rather than suppressed ones, so you have to run the second premise to see that it connects.

choices.note: Tempting, because it uses all the right words. But it reverses the first premise: No live virus → Safe. It still never tells us anything about Velmar.
This reverses the second premise (Suppressed → mostly transplant) and still doesn't mention Velmar. No link to the conclusion.
Wrong group. Patients with normal immune systems aren't covered by the 'only' rule, so being safe for them tells us nothing about live virus.
Tempting, but it only helps if Velmar was approved for transplant patients, which nobody says. Velmar could be approved only for other people.

CORRECT. If Velmar is safe for some recent transplant patient, that patient has a suppressed immune system, and only no-live-virus vaccines are safe for such patients. So Velmar contains no live virus.

questions.stimulus: According to Arden Farm's records, most of the strawberries the farm loses each year are eaten by birds; only a small share are spoiled by mold. So the proposal to spray the farm's strawberry fields with a costly fungicide each spring will not substantially reduce the amount of fruit the farm loses each year.
questions.stem: Which one of the following arguments is most similar in its pattern of reasoning to the argument above?
choices: Most of the noise complaints in Ellery come from residents who live near the airport rather than near the highway. So the noise in Ellery is worse near the airport than near the highway.
Most of the traffic accidents in the town of Pell occur on weekends. So the plan to add extra police patrols on weekends will substantially reduce the total number of traffic accidents in Pell.
Most of the books returned late to the Hadley library are children's books. So the library should extend its loan period for children's books by at least a week.
Most of the water lost from the Halston reservoir evaporates; only a little leaks through the old dam. So repairing the dam will not substantially reduce the amount of water the reservoir loses.
Most of the trees in Ardell Park are oaks, and most oaks lose their leaves in the fall. So most of the trees in Ardell Park lose their leaves in the fall.
questions.explanation: The argument reasons that because a proposal addresses only a minor cause of a loss, it won't substantially reduce the loss; (D) does the same with a dam repair that addresses only the minor cause of water loss. (B) is tempting because it also concerns a plan aimed at a share of a problem, but it targets the main share and concludes the plan will work. (E) is a quantifier argument with no plan or causes.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Spraying fungicide each spring won't substantially reduce the farm's yearly strawberry losses.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Most losses come from birds; only a small share come from mold.

setup.label: Pattern
