setup.text: Most of loss L comes from cause A; only a little comes from cause B; so a plan that addresses only B won't substantially reduce L.

breakdown.analysis: Strip it down: two causes of a problem, one big and one small; the proposal tackles only the small one; so it won't make a big dent. Match every piece: a loss, a major cause, a minor cause, a plan aimed at the minor cause, and a 'won't substantially reduce' conclusion.

choices.note: No plan and no causes of a loss. It moves from where complaints come from to where noise is worse. Different structure.
Tempting, because it has a 'most' and a plan. But the plan targets the main share and concludes it will work. That's the reverse of the original's 'targets the minor share, won't work.'
Ends in a recommendation ('should extend'), and the plan targets the major share. Different conclusion type.
CORRECT. Major cause (evaporation), minor cause (leaks), plan addresses only the minor one (repair the dam), so it won't substantially reduce the loss. Piece for piece the same.
A 'most + most' quantifier chain about trees. No plan, no causes, no reduction. Completely different (and flawed) structure.

passages.title: Poets’ recordings of their own work
passages.subject: humanities
passages.text:
Archives now hold thousands of recordings of poets reading their own work, and a growing number of scholars treat these recordings as the surest guide to how the poems should sound. Print, these scholars point out, fixes a poem’s words but leaves much of their timing open: a reader confronting an irregular line must decide where the stresses fall, how long to pause at a line break, and whether a dash marks a hesitation or a rush. On such matters, they argue, the poet’s own voice is the best evidence we will ever have—the closest thing we have to a score. Their favorite example is Hedda Morrow, whose 1958 collection Tidewater was long faulted for its “shapeless” free verse. In recordings Morrow made for a regional radio station in 1960, she reads nearly every line with four strong beats, pausing so deliberately at line ends that the apparent shapelessness disappears. The pattern, the argument runs, was there all along; the page simply failed to show it.

The recordings are invaluable, but they deserve more caution than this argument allows. A poet reading aloud is a performer, and performances answer to circumstance. Calloway Ness recorded his poem “Harbor Psalm” three times over twenty years: slowly and evenly in 1949, briskly in 1957, and in 1968, before a large audience, with long dramatic pauses that appear in neither earlier version. Which of these is the poem’s true rhythm? To privilege any one of them is to choose, not to discover. Nor is a poet necessarily a skilled reader. Some poets have admitted, in interviews and letters, to reading in a flat, hurried manner they find uncomfortable to hear, and nervousness before a microphone may alter a reading in ways that have nothing to do with the verse.

Moreover, a published poem addresses readers who will never hear the poet’s voice, and the page has resources of its own—line breaks, spacing, punctuation—that the poet chose deliberately. When a recording seems to override these, it is at least as plausible that the poet was improvising as that the page was deficient. Morrow’s pauses tell us how she chose to perform Tidewater for a radio audience in 1960; whether they reveal a pattern the poems possessed from the start is a separate question. None of this makes recordings irrelevant. A reading documents one way a poem was understood by someone who knew it intimately, and it can alert us to possibilities a silent reader might miss. Where a poet’s several readings agree with one another and with the evidence of the page, they can rightly strengthen our confidence in an interpretation. But it is evidence to be weighed alongside the page, not a verdict to be obeyed.

passages.title: Brandt and the end of Halvern’s volunteer fire companies
passages.subject: social-science
passages.text:
Through most of the nineteenth century, the towns of the Halvern province relied for protection against fire on volunteer companies: associations of tradesmen and shopkeepers who drilled together, maintained a hand-drawn engine, and answered the alarm bell without pay. Between 1870 and 1900 nearly all of these companies were disbanded and replaced by salaried municipal departments. The standard explanation holds that the volunteers simply could not keep pace with the growth of the towns: as buildings rose higher and streets multiplied, fires outstripped what part-time crews could control.

The historian Anika Brandt finds this explanation unpersuasive. Volunteer companies, she notes, were often quick to acquire new equipment, including steam-powered pumps, and municipal records give little indication that fire losses in Halvern’s towns rose in the years before the changeover. What changed, in Brandt’s view, was the market for fire insurance. As large insurers based in the provincial capital extended their business into the smaller towns, they began setting premiums according to the kind of protection a town provided, and they offered substantially lower rates in towns that maintained a paid department. Merchants and property owners—the very people who filled the volunteer ranks—thus acquired a direct financial interest in abolishing their own companies. Brandt’s account has the considerable merit of explaining the timing of the change, which the standard view leaves obscure: in town after town, the disbanding of the volunteer company followed the arrival of the large insurers, sometimes within a few years. It also explains why, as council minutes show, members of the volunteer companies themselves frequently proposed the measures that ended their companies.

Yet the account leaves an important question unanswered: why did the insurers prefer paid departments? Brandt treats the insurers’ rate schedules as though they simply recorded a judgment about which kind of department fought fires better—but she has herself argued that there is little evidence the volunteers fought fires worse. If the insurers’ preference was not grounded in performance, it may have rested on something else: perhaps the fact that a salaried department, answerable to a town council, could be held to written standards of readiness, whereas a volunteer company’s obligations were matters of custom and honor. Such an explanation would be compatible with Brandt’s central claim, but it would shift its emphasis, locating the decisive change not in the insurance market as such but in a broader preference, shared by insurers and councils alike, for obligations that could be specified and enforced.

Nor does Brandt account for the handful of towns, such as Orrisby, that kept their volunteer companies into the 1910s despite paying higher premiums. Until such exceptions are explained, her account, though a considerable improvement on its predecessor, cannot be regarded as complete.

passages.title: Ferreira on the Dolan test for suggestive identifications
passages.subject: law
passages.text:
In the courts of Calvery, an eyewitness identification obtained through a suggestive police procedure—showing the witness a single suspect rather than a lineup, for example, or telling the witness after a selection that she has picked the right person—is not automatically excluded from trial. Under the rule announced in Regina v. Dolan (1979), a judge who finds a procedure unnecessarily suggestive must nonetheless admit the identification if, considering all the circumstances, it appears reliable. Among the circumstances the court listed were the witness’s opportunity to view the offender, the witness’s degree of attention, and the certainty the witness expresses.

The legal scholar Anouk Ferreira has argued that the Dolan test defeats itself, because its reliability factors are not independent of the suggestion they are meant to offset. Research on memory has established that a witness who receives confirming feedback after choosing someone (“Good, you identified our suspect”) typically becomes more confident in the choice and, asked later, tends to report a better view and closer attention than witnesses given no such feedback. A suggestive procedure can thus inflate the very measures a court consults to decide whether the suggestion did harm, so that the worse the procedure, the more reliable the resulting identification may appear. The test, in Ferreira’s phrase, is “a thermometer that the fever itself can reset.” She concludes that any identification obtained through an unnecessarily suggestive procedure should be excluded.

Ferreira’s diagnosis is difficult to resist. A witness’s certainty as stated on the stand, months after the procedure, tells a court more about what has happened to the witness’s memory since the identification than about the identification itself. But her remedy sweeps more broadly than her diagnosis requires. Excluding every such identification would discard some that are very likely accurate—that of a witness who picks a longtime neighbor out of a fair lineup as the offender, for instance, and is then told that she has chosen the suspect. And her argument shows only that the Dolan factors, as courts now measure them, are contaminated; it does not show that no uncontaminated measure exists.

Suppose police were required to record, in the witness’s own words and at the moment of the first identification, how confident she was and how well she had seen and attended to the offender. Such a record would be fixed before the confirming remarks Ferreira describes could act on it, and a court could consult it instead of the witness’s later testimony. Admittedly, such a record would not cure every suggestive procedure: a witness shown a single suspect is steered toward a choice before any confidence can be stated, and for procedures of that kind Ferreira’s strictness may well be warranted. But for the distortion on which her critique chiefly rests, a reformed test, not exclusion, is the proportionate response.

passages.title: Winged seeds in Tessel’s campion
passages.subject: natural-science
passages.text:
Tessel’s campion, a low upland perennial, bears two kinds of seed: heavy seeds that fall close to the parent and lighter seeds fringed with a papery wing that the wind can carry tens of meters. Botanists long assumed that the winged seeds served chiefly to carry the species into newly opened ground, such as fresh rockfalls on steep slopes. A 1998 survey by the botanist Ruth Aldane therefore came as a puzzle. Aldane found that plants on steep, frequently disturbed slopes devoted only about 15 percent of their seeds to the winged form, whereas plants in the dense, stable meadows of the valley floors devoted nearly half.

Aldane’s explanation centered on competition among relatives. In a crowded meadow, a seed that falls beside its parent must compete for one of a few small gaps in the turf, and its most likely competitors are its own siblings. Suppose a parent drops forty heavy seeds around it and two gaps open there in a season: at most two of the forty can establish, and the rest are lost. A winged seed that lands elsewhere competes mostly with the offspring of other plants, so each one that reaches a gap adds to the parent’s descendants rather than replacing a sibling that would have taken the gap anyway. On a disturbed slope the arithmetic is different: open ground near the parent is plentiful, so heavy seeds dropped nearby are seldom wasted.

Aldane’s account implied that the plants could detect crowding. In a greenhouse, she raised seedlings from both habitats in pots at high and low densities. Plants grown crowded produced a high proportion of winged seeds and plants grown sparsely a low one, regardless of whether their parents had come from meadow or slope. The difference between the habitats, then, was not inherited but a response to each plant’s conditions.

How the plants sense crowding was clarified in 2010 by Tomas Ferrel. Leaves absorb red light strongly but transmit and reflect much of the far-red, so light that has passed through or bounced off neighboring foliage is relatively poor in red. Growing campion without neighbors under adjustable lamps, Ferrel found that a low ratio of red to far-red light alone raised the proportion of winged seeds to meadow levels, whereas merely dimming the lamps had no effect. Yet the cue is imperfect. Campion growing beneath young birch on the slopes, where the canopy filters the light but open ground is plentiful, produces winged seeds in meadow proportions. Aldane’s account has held up well, but such cases suggest a refinement: the campion responds not to crowding itself but to a signal that ordinarily accompanies crowding, and where the two come apart, the plant’s allocation may serve it poorly. Whether the birch-shaded plants actually suffer for it has yet to be measured.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?
choices: Recordings of poets reading their own work are the best available evidence of how a poem’s lines should be timed and stressed, and scholars should consult them whenever they exist.
Because poets’ readings of their own work vary with circumstance, recordings of those readings have no legitimate role in determining how a poem should be read.
Recordings of poets reading their own work are valuable evidence about how the poems may sound, but they should be weighed alongside the printed text rather than treated as authoritative.
The case of Hedda Morrow shows that critics who judge free verse solely from the printed page are likely to mistake a deliberate pattern of stresses for shapelessness.
Poets are frequently unskilled readers of their own work, so a poem’s printed text is a more reliable guide to its rhythm than any recording the poet has made.
questions.explanation: The first paragraph reports other scholars’ view that a poet’s recording is the best evidence of a poem’s rhythm; from the second paragraph on, the author argues that recordings are valuable but must be weighed alongside the page, not obeyed. That is C. A is the trap: it states the scholars’ position, not the author’s. B and E overshoot, since the author says recordings are not irrelevant and never ranks the page above them.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: State the author’s main point.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The first paragraph (the scholars’ view), the first sentence of the second paragraph, and the last four sentences of the passage.

breakdown.analysis: Whose view is the first paragraph? Not the author’s: “these scholars point out,” “they argue,” “the argument runs.” The author’s own voice arrives at the start of the second paragraph: recordings are “invaluable, but they deserve more caution than this argument allows.” The end of the passage pins it down: recordings aren’t irrelevant, but they’re “evidence to be weighed alongside the page, not a verdict to be obeyed.” We need an answer that says: valuable, but not the final word.

choices.note: Tempting, because it fills a whole paragraph of the passage. But it’s the scholars’ view, which the author spends the rest of the passage qualifying. A main point question wants the author’s position, not the view the author is responding to.
Too strong. The author does say readings vary with circumstance, but the third paragraph says flatly, “None of this makes recordings irrelevant.”
CORRECT. Valuable (“invaluable,” “not irrelevant”) but not authoritative (“evidence to be weighed alongside the page, not a verdict to be obeyed”). That’s the author’s position, qualifier included.

This is the scholars’ reading of one example, and the author actually doubts it: Morrow’s pauses may show only how she “chose to perform” the poems in 1960. Even if it were right, it would be one detail, not the main point.
Too strong, and it adds a ranking the author never makes. The author says some poets read poorly and that the page has resources of its own, but never puts the page above every recording.

questions.stem: The passage mentions which one of the following as something that may alter a poet’s reading of his or her own work in ways unrelated to the poem itself?
choices: nervousness that the poet feels before a microphone
the poet’s familiarity with recordings made by other poets
revisions the poet has made to the printed text since publication
the quality of the equipment used to make the recording
the opinions of critics who have reviewed the poet’s collection
questions.explanation: The last sentence of the second paragraph says that “nervousness before a microphone may alter a reading in ways that have nothing to do with the verse,” which is A. D is the likeliest slip because it also concerns the recording situation, but the passage never mentions equipment; B, C, and E are likewise never raised.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the influence on a reading that the passage actually names.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The last sentence of the second paragraph.

breakdown.analysis: Pure detail, so go back and find it instead of trusting memory. The last sentence of the second paragraph: “nervousness before a microphone may alter a reading in ways that have nothing to do with the verse.” That matches the stem almost word for word. The wrong answers will sound like things that could affect a reading in real life, but the passage never mentions them. Stated beats plausible.

choices.note: CORRECT. The last sentence of the second paragraph: nervousness before a microphone “may alter a reading in ways that have nothing to do with the verse.”
Never mentioned. The passage says nothing about poets listening to one another’s recordings.
Never mentioned. The passage discusses the page’s line breaks and punctuation, not revisions to the text.
Tempting, because it’s also about the recording situation. But the passage never mentions equipment. Plausible in real life isn’t the same as stated.
Never raised as an influence on a reading. The only critics in the passage are the ones who called Tidewater shapeless, and nothing says they affected how Morrow read.

questions.stem: By describing a poet’s recorded voice as “the closest thing we have to a score” (third sentence of the first paragraph), the scholars discussed in the passage most probably mean that such a recording
choices: is, like a musical score, consulted mainly by specialists rather than by the general readers to whom a poem is addressed
shows that a poem, like a piece of music, cannot be fully appreciated by a reader who has never heard it performed aloud
should, like a musical score, be revised by later performers whenever its markings prove inadequate to the work
indicates that poets ought to set their verse to music if they wish its rhythm to be preserved for future readers
comes nearer than any other available source to fixing exactly how the poem’s lines are meant to be timed and stressed
questions.explanation: A score tells performers how a piece is to be timed and stressed. The scholars hold that print leaves timing open and that the poet’s voice is the best evidence about stresses and pauses, so calling the recording the closest thing to a score means it comes nearer than any other source to fixing that timing: E. B is the tempting trap, but the scholars’ point concerns evidence of intended rhythm, not whether poems must be heard to be appreciated.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Explain what the scholars mean by calling the recording a “score.”

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The second and third sentences of the first paragraph.

breakdown.analysis: What does a musical score do? It tells performers how a piece is to be timed and stressed. Now read the sentence before the phrase: print “leaves much of their timing open” (stresses, pauses at line breaks, what a dash means). So the recording is the nearest thing to a document that fixes that timing. “Closest thing” matters too: not a perfect score, just the best available. We need: comes nearest to specifying how the lines should be timed. Meaning-in-context traps take the metaphor too literally; watch for actual music.

choices.note: Picks up the score image but adds something the passage never says: who consults recordings. The comparison is about what a score specifies, not about its audience.
Tempting. It runs with the music comparison. But the scholars’ claim is about evidence of intended timing, not about whether a poem can be appreciated in silence.
Nothing in the passage is about revising recordings. This borrows a feature of musical practice and pins it on the recording.
Takes the metaphor literally. Nobody in the passage suggests setting poems to music.
CORRECT. Print leaves timing open; the recording comes nearest to fixing it. “Closest thing” means nearer than any other available source, not a perfect record.

questions.stem: The author discusses Calloway Ness’s three recordings of “Harbor Psalm” (second paragraph) primarily in order to
choices: show that recordings made before large audiences are less trustworthy than those a poet makes in a studio
support the claim that a poet’s readings vary with circumstance and so cannot fix a single true rhythm
suggest that a poet’s understanding of a poem’s rhythm grows more accurate as the poet returns to it over the years
illustrate the claim that some poets read their own work in a flat, hurried manner they find uncomfortable to hear
demonstrate that the printed text of “Harbor Psalm” fails to indicate the rhythm its author intended for it
questions.explanation: The example follows the claim that “performances answer to circumstance” and is followed by “To privilege any one of them is to choose, not to discover.” Three different readings of one poem show that no single reading fixes the poem’s true rhythm, which is B. D is the trap: it describes the next point, introduced with “Nor” as a separate consideration.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Say why the author brings up the three recordings.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The second through fifth sentences of the second paragraph.

breakdown.analysis: Why-mention questions are answered by the sentences around the example. Before it: “performances answer to circumstance.” After it: “Which of these is the poem’s true rhythm? To privilege any one of them is to choose, not to discover.” So the example is evidence that readings shift with the occasion, and the lesson drawn is that no single reading can be crowned the true rhythm.

choices.note: The 1968 reading was before a large audience, but the author never ranks it below the others. The point is that the three differ, not that one is worse.
CORRECT. The example backs “performances answer to circumstance,” and the author draws the lesson: privileging any one reading “is to choose, not to discover.”
Nothing suggests the later readings are better. The author asks which one is the true rhythm and refuses to pick.
Tempting, because that claim comes right after the example. But it’s introduced with “Nor,” as a separate consideration. The Ness example is about variation across occasions, not poor reading skill.
The author never says the printed text of “Harbor Psalm” is deficient. If anything, the third paragraph defends the page’s own resources.

questions.stem: With which one of the following statements about Hedda Morrow’s 1960 recordings would the author be most likely to agree?
choices: They show that the critics who called Tidewater shapeless were relying on a careless reading of the printed poems.
They should be set aside entirely by any scholar who is attempting to describe the rhythm of the poems in Tidewater.
They prove that Morrow did not have any regular pattern of stresses in mind when she composed the poems in Tidewater.
They show how Morrow chose to perform the poems for radio in 1960 without settling whether the poems themselves are patterned.
They are less reliable than Morrow’s later readings would have been, since she was then unaccustomed to reading for radio.
questions.explanation: The third sentence of the third paragraph reads: Morrow’s pauses “tell us how she chose to perform Tidewater for a radio audience in 1960; whether they reveal a pattern the poems possessed from the start is a separate question.” That is D. C overshoots in one direction (the author leaves the question open) and B in the other (the author says recordings are not irrelevant).

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the author’s own view of the Morrow recordings.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The end of the first paragraph (the scholars’ use of Morrow) and the third and fourth sentences of the third paragraph (the author’s reply).

breakdown.analysis: The scholars use Morrow to say the pattern “was there all along.” The author answers in the third sentence of the third paragraph: the pauses “tell us how she chose to perform Tidewater for a radio audience in 1960; whether they reveal a pattern the poems possessed from the start is a separate question.” So: a record of one performance, not proof about the poems. And the very next sentence stops the author from going further: recordings aren’t irrelevant. Expect traps on both sides of that middle position.

choices.note: The author never evaluates how the critics read the page. Calling them careless pushes the scholars’ line even further; it isn’t the author’s view.
Too strong. “None of this makes recordings irrelevant.” The author wants them weighed, not discarded.
Too strong in the other direction. The author says the question of the poems’ pattern is open (“a separate question”), not that Morrow had no pattern in mind.
CORRECT. This paraphrases the third sentence of the third paragraph: the recordings document a 1960 performance, and whether they reveal the poems’ own pattern “is a separate question.”
Nothing in the passage compares Morrow’s 1960 readings with later ones or says she was new to radio. Made up.

questions.stem: The author’s argument in the second paragraph most directly challenges which one of the following assumptions on which the argument of the scholars described in the first paragraph relies?
choices: How a poet reads a poem aloud is determined by the poem itself rather than by the occasion of the reading.
The rhythm of a poem is relevant to how the poem ought to be interpreted by its readers.
The printed page gives a reader no reliable guidance about how long to pause at the end of a line of verse.
Free verse is more likely than regular meter to be misjudged when it is read only on the page.
Recordings made for radio broadcast are generally prepared with more care than recordings made before a live audience.
questions.explanation: The scholars infer from Morrow’s four-beat readings that ‘the pattern was there all along,’ which requires that a poet’s reading be governed by the poem rather than by the occasion; the second paragraph attacks exactly this with ‘performances answer to circumstance,’ the three Ness recordings, and nervousness at the microphone. That is A. C is the trap: the author does push back on the page’s supposed silence, but in the third paragraph (‘the page has resources of its own’), not the second, and C is stronger than the scholars’ own claim that print ‘leaves much of their timing open.’ B is an assumption the author shares.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find an assumption the scholars need that the SECOND paragraph, specifically, attacks.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The first paragraph (the scholars’ argument from Morrow) and the second paragraph (‘performances answer to circumstance’; Ness; nervousness). Check the third paragraph only to rule out the trap.

breakdown.analysis: Two tests: (1) the scholars must rely on it, and (2) the second paragraph must hit it. So what if Morrow read four beats on the radio? Does that show the poems have four beats? Only if a reading is governed by the poem and not by the day, the audience, or the poet’s nerves. The second paragraph attacks exactly that. Prephrase: a poet’s reading reflects the poem, not the circumstances. The key says this abstractly, with no mention of Morrow or recordings. Most students pick (C) because the author really does dispute the idea that the page is silent about timing. It fails twice: that rebuttal (‘the page has resources of its own—line breaks, spacing, punctuation’) is in the third paragraph, and ‘no reliable guidance’ is stronger than the scholars’ actual claim that print ‘leaves much of their timing open.’ Read the locator in the stem as a hard limit.

choices.note: CORRECT. The scholars need this to move from how Morrow performed to how the poems are built, and the second paragraph targets it head-on: readings ‘answer to circumstance,’ Ness read one poem three ways, and nerves alter readings.
The scholars do assume rhythm matters, but so does the author, who cares about line breaks and punctuation for that reason. Passes test 1, fails test 2.

Tempting. The author does defend the page, so this feels like something the author challenges. But that defense is in the third paragraph, not the second, and the scholars claim only that print ‘leaves much of their timing open,’ not that it gives no reliable guidance.
Nobody compares free verse with regular meter. Morrow’s verse is free verse, but that’s just a feature of the example.
No one ranks radio recordings above live ones. The radio station and the large audience are details of the examples, not premises.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?
choices: The volunteer fire companies of Halvern were disbanded because, as the towns grew, the volunteers could no longer control the fires that broke out in them.
Brandt’s insurance-based explanation of the end of Halvern’s volunteer fire companies improves on the standard view but still leaves some important questions unanswered.
Insurers in Halvern preferred paid fire departments because such departments had been shown to fight fires more effectively than the volunteer companies they replaced.
Brandt’s explanation of the end of Halvern’s volunteer fire companies must be rejected, because it cannot account for towns such as Orrisby that kept their volunteers.
The volunteer companies of Halvern declined because insurers and town councils alike preferred obligations that could be specified and enforced to those resting on custom.
questions.explanation: The passage presents the standard explanation, Brandt’s insurance-based alternative and its merits, and then two gaps: why insurers preferred paid departments, and towns like Orrisby. B captures this. D overstates the author’s criticism (incomplete, not mistaken), and E promotes the author’s tentative “perhaps” suggestion to the passage’s conclusion.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: State the main point.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The first sentence of the second paragraph, the first sentence of the third paragraph, and the last sentence of the passage.

breakdown.analysis: Map it. First paragraph: background plus the standard explanation. Second: Brandt rejects it, offers the insurance account, and the author praises what that account explains. Third: a gap (why did insurers prefer paid departments?). Fourth: another gap (Orrisby), ending “a considerable improvement on its predecessor, cannot be regarded as complete.” That last sentence is basically the main point: better than the old view, but incomplete.

choices.note: That’s the standard explanation, which Brandt rejects and the author never defends.
CORRECT. Better than its predecessor, with open questions. It tracks the passage’s last sentence: “a considerable improvement on its predecessor … cannot be regarded as complete.”
Contradicts the passage. Brandt argues there is “little evidence the volunteers fought fires worse,” and the author builds on that point.
Too strong. The author calls the account incomplete and “a considerable improvement.” Incomplete isn’t the same as rejected.
Tempting, but this is the author’s “perhaps” suggestion from the third paragraph, offered as a possible refinement. It isn’t the passage’s conclusion.

questions.stem: According to the passage, Brandt cites which one of the following as evidence against the standard explanation?
choices: Merchants and property owners made up much of the membership of the volunteer companies.
Insurers offered substantially lower premiums to towns that maintained salaried departments.
Some towns, such as Orrisby, kept their volunteer companies well into the 1910s.
Volunteer companies were often quick to acquire new equipment, such as steam pumps.
Buildings in Halvern’s towns grew taller and more numerous in the late nineteenth century.
questions.explanation: Right after calling the standard explanation unpersuasive, Brandt notes that volunteer companies “were often quick to acquire new equipment, including steam-powered pumps,” and that fire losses did not seem to rise. That is D. B is the tempting trap: Brandt relies on it, but as support for her own account, not against the standard one; C is the author’s point against Brandt.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find what Brandt offers against the standard explanation.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The first two sentences of the second paragraph.

breakdown.analysis: The stem is specific: evidence against the standard explanation, not evidence for Brandt’s own view. The second paragraph opens with Brandt calling the standard view “unpersuasive” and then she “notes” two things: volunteers were quick to get new equipment, including steam pumps, and fire losses didn’t seem to rise before the changeover. One of those should be in the choices. Expect traps that are things Brandt says for a different purpose.

choices.note: Brandt does use this, but as part of her own explanation: the people in the volunteer ranks had a financial stake in ending their companies. It isn’t aimed at the standard view.
Tempting. Brandt relies on it, but as support for her insurance account, not as evidence that the volunteers could keep up. Right author, wrong job.
Wrong person and wrong target. The author raises Orrisby in the last paragraph, and against Brandt.

CORRECT. Right after calling the standard explanation unpersuasive, Brandt notes that volunteer companies “were often quick to acquire new equipment.” That cuts against the claim that they couldn’t keep pace.
This is part of the standard explanation’s own story (“buildings rose higher”), not evidence against it, and the passage doesn’t present it as something Brandt cites.

questions.stem: In describing a volunteer company’s obligations as “matters of custom and honor” (third sentence of the third paragraph), the author most likely means that these obligations
choices: were taken less seriously by volunteers than paid firefighters took their own contractual duties
were passed down within families from one generation of volunteers to the next
rested on unwritten expectations rather than on standards that could be formally enforced
were regarded by the insurers as more dependable than any written standard of readiness
had been imposed on the companies by town councils in exchange for public funding
questions.explanation: The phrase is set against a salaried department that “could be held to written standards of readiness” and against “obligations that could be specified and enforced.” Obligations of custom and honor are real but unwritten and not formally enforceable, which is C. A is the tempting trap, but the author implies nothing about how seriously volunteers took their duties.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Explain the phrase by what it is contrasted with.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The third and fourth sentences of the third paragraph.

breakdown.analysis: Read what the phrase is set against. A salaried department, “answerable to a town council, could be held to written standards of readiness, whereas” the volunteers’ obligations were custom and honor. The paragraph then sums up with “obligations that could be specified and enforced.” So custom and honor = real obligations, but unwritten and not formally enforceable. Watch for the trap that reads the phrase as an insult to the volunteers.

choices.note: Tempting, because “custom and honor” can sound soft. But the author says nothing about how seriously volunteers took their duties, only about whether those duties could be specified and enforced.
Reads “custom” as family tradition. The passage never mentions families or inheritance; the contrast is with written standards.
CORRECT. The phrase is set against “written standards of readiness” and “obligations that could be specified and enforced.” Unwritten, and so not formally enforceable.
Backwards. The author suggests insurers preferred paid departments precisely because their obligations were written.
Backwards again. It’s the paid department that is “answerable to a town council.” Nothing says councils imposed the volunteers’ obligations, and funding is never mentioned.

questions.stem: The passage most strongly suggests that the standard explanation would have difficulty accounting for which one of the following?
choices: that the towns of Halvern grew substantially in size during the second half of the nineteenth century
that fires became harder for part-time crews to control as buildings in Halvern’s towns rose higher
that the volunteer companies were made up largely of tradesmen and shopkeepers who served without pay
that a few towns, such as Orrisby, kept their volunteer companies despite paying higher insurance premiums
that towns tended to disband their volunteer companies soon after the large insurers had arrived
questions.explanation: In the second paragraph the author credits Brandt’s account with explaining “the timing of the change, which the standard view leaves obscure”: disbanding followed the insurers’ arrival, sometimes within a few years. That is E. D is the trap: the author raises Orrisby as a problem for Brandt, not for the standard view; A and B are part of the standard explanation itself.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find a fact the standard explanation can’t handle well.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The second-to-last sentence of the second paragraph.

breakdown.analysis: The passage hands you this one. In the second paragraph the author says Brandt’s account explains “the timing of the change, which the standard view leaves obscure”: disbanding followed the insurers’ arrival, town by town, sometimes within a few years. Ask the blunt question: if the volunteers were simply overwhelmed by growth, why would the end come right after the insurers showed up? The standard view has no answer.

choices.note: This is part of the standard explanation’s own story. Growth is what it uses to explain the change.
Again, this is the standard explanation itself, not a problem for it.
Neutral background from the first paragraph. Nothing about it is awkward for the standard view.

Tempting, because the passage does call Orrisby an unexplained exception. But it’s raised against Brandt’s account, not the standard one. A growth-based view could handle Orrisby easily if Orrisby grew little.
CORRECT. The author says this timing, disbanding soon after the insurers arrived, is something “the standard view leaves obscure.”

questions.stem: The primary function of the third paragraph is to
choices: raise a difficulty in Brandt’s account and suggest an explanation that would refine rather than overturn it
present new evidence that undermines Brandt’s central claim about the role played by the provincial insurance market
argue that the standard explanation of the change was correct after all, despite Brandt’s objections
describe in some detail the procedure by which the large insurers set premiums for the towns of Halvern
establish that volunteer companies fought fires at least as effectively as paid departments did
questions.explanation: The third paragraph asks why insurers preferred paid departments, notes that Brandt treats the rates as a judgment about performance even though she argued the volunteers were no worse, and offers, with “perhaps,” a suggestion that the author says “would be compatible with Brandt’s central claim” but would shift its emphasis. That is A. B is the tempting trap, but the author expressly says the suggestion refines rather than undermines Brandt.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Describe what the third paragraph does.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The third paragraph, especially its first and last sentences.

breakdown.analysis: Map the paragraph. It opens with a question Brandt leaves unanswered (why did insurers prefer paid departments?), points out a tension (she treats the rates as a judgment about performance, but she herself argued the volunteers weren’t worse), offers a “perhaps” answer (enforceable written standards), and closes by saying that answer “would be compatible with Brandt’s central claim” but would shift its emphasis. So: a difficulty plus a friendly refinement.

choices.note: CORRECT. The difficulty is the unanswered question and the tension inside Brandt’s account; the suggestion about enforceable obligations is “compatible with Brandt’s central claim” but shifts its emphasis. Refine, not overturn.

Tempting, because the paragraph does criticize Brandt. But the author explicitly says the suggestion is compatible with her central claim. And there’s no new evidence, just a question and a “perhaps.”
The standard explanation doesn’t come up in this paragraph, and the author never revives it.
The paragraph mentions rate schedules but never describes how premiums were set. It asks why insurers preferred paid departments, not how rates were calculated.
That’s Brandt’s point from the second paragraph, which this paragraph mentions only in passing. And she claimed “little evidence” of worse performance, not proof of equal performance.

questions.stem: Which one of the following is most analogous to the situation that, according to Brandt, led to the disbanding of Halvern’s volunteer fire companies?
choices: Members of a neighborhood watch group disband it after the city hires additional police officers, because they feel the group is no longer needed.
A volunteer ambulance corps is replaced by a paid service after a series of well-publicized delays in its response to emergencies.
A town’s merchants form a volunteer street-cleaning association after the town council reduces the budget for municipal sanitation services.
Farmers vote to close their cooperative grain store after lenders begin offering cheaper loans to those farmers who use licensed commercial storage.
A volunteer library committee hires a professional librarian after its members, many of them retirees, find the work increasingly difficult to keep up.
questions.explanation: Brandt’s account: an outside party offers better prices when a service is run by paid professionals, giving the members of a voluntary association a financial reason to abolish it themselves. D matches every element: lenders favor licensed storage, so the farmers close their own cooperative. B and E are performance stories, the skeleton of the standard explanation Brandt rejects.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Match the structure of Brandt’s explanation.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The third through fifth sentences of the second paragraph.

breakdown.analysis: Strip Brandt’s account to its skeleton: 1. an outside party (insurers) charges less when a service is provided by paid professionals; 2. that gives the members of a voluntary association a financial reason to end it; 3. so the members themselves abolish their own association. Notice what’s NOT in the skeleton: the volunteers doing a worse job. Analogy traps match some elements but not all, so check each one.

choices.note: The members end their own group, but because it isn’t needed anymore, not because an outside party’s prices gave them a financial stake. The core element is missing.
This is the skeleton of the standard explanation (the volunteers couldn’t perform), which Brandt rejects.
Reverses the direction: a volunteer group is created, not dissolved, and there’s no outside pricing incentive.
CORRECT. An outside party (lenders) prices in favor of a professional alternative (licensed storage), so the members themselves vote to close their own cooperative. Every element matches.
Tempting, because a volunteer group turns to a paid professional. But the cause is the members’ difficulty doing the work, a performance story, and no outside party’s prices are involved.

questions.stem: The author would be most likely to agree with which one of the following statements about the insurers’ rate schedules (second sentence of the third paragraph)?
choices: They show that the insurers knew more about local fire losses than the town councils did.
Brandt’s reading of them is in tension with a conclusion she reaches elsewhere in her own argument.
They charged the same premium to every town that kept its volunteer company into the 1910s.
They reflected the insurers’ preference for departments that could be held to written standards of readiness.
They had little influence on the decisions of town councils to disband their volunteer companies.
questions.explanation: The author says Brandt treats the rate schedules as a judgment about which kind of department fought fires better, ‘but she has herself argued that there is little evidence the volunteers fought fires worse’; her reading of the schedules conflicts with her own earlier conclusion, B. D is the trap: the written-standards idea is the author’s own suggestion, but it is offered only as a ‘perhaps’ about what the preference ‘may have rested on,’ so the author would not flatly assert it. E contradicts Brandt’s central claim, which the author accepts; A and C are unsupported details.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the author’s view of the insurers’ rate schedules, at the strength the author holds it.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The first three sentences of the third paragraph; the second sentence of the second paragraph for Brandt’s claim about how well the volunteers fought fires.

breakdown.analysis: What does the author actually say about the rate schedules? One thing for sure: Brandt reads them as a verdict on firefighting performance, ‘but she has herself argued that there is little evidence the volunteers fought fires worse.’ That ‘but’ marks a tension inside Brandt’s own account. The key says this in stand-in form (‘a conclusion she reaches elsewhere’), so you have to trace it back to the second paragraph. Most students pick (D) because it is the author’s own idea, so it feels like the author’s view. It fails on strength: the author says the preference ‘may have rested on something else: perhaps’ written standards. A ‘perhaps’ is not an assertion. Watch the move from a possibility to a fact.

choices.note: Nothing in the passage compares what insurers and councils knew about fire losses. Made up.

CORRECT. Brandt reads the schedules as a judgment that paid departments fought fires better, yet she herself argued there is little evidence the volunteers fought worse. That is the tension the author’s ‘but’ points out.
The passage says towns like Orrisby paid higher premiums, never that every such town paid the same premium. Unsupported detail.

Tempting, because the written-standards idea is the author’s. But the author offers it only as what the preference ‘may have rested on’: ‘perhaps.’ This states as fact what the author floats as a possibility.
Contradicts Brandt’s central claim, which the author accepts as ‘a considerable improvement.’ The author never doubts that the premiums mattered.

questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, would most call into question Brandt’s account as it is described in the passage?
choices: Volunteer companies in Halvern frequently held public dinners to raise money for the purchase of new equipment.
The insurers’ preference for paid departments did not rest on any evidence that such departments fought fires better.
Fire losses in Halvern’s towns declined noticeably in the years after salaried municipal departments were established.
Some members of disbanded volunteer companies later joined the paid departments that replaced them as salaried firefighters.
Most merchants in Halvern’s smaller towns insured through mutual societies whose rates ignored a town’s fire protection.
questions.explanation: Brandt’s account runs: the large insurers offered lower premiums for paid departments, so the merchants and property owners who filled the volunteer ranks acquired a financial interest in abolishing their own companies. E says most merchants were not insured on such terms at all, which cuts the link between the premiums and the people who voted the companies out. B is the trap: it echoes the author’s own objection, but the author says such a point ‘would be compatible with Brandt’s central claim,’ so it does not undermine her account. C concerns results after the change, not its cause.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the fact that most damages Brandt’s account of why the volunteer companies were disbanded.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The second paragraph (Brandt’s causal chain: insurers → premiums → merchants’ interest → disbanding) and the last sentence of the third paragraph (what the author says is ‘compatible with Brandt’s central claim’).

breakdown.analysis: Brandt’s account is a chain: 1. large insurers arrive; 2. their premiums favor paid departments; 3. so merchants, who are the volunteers, gain ‘a direct financial interest’ in abolishing their own companies; 4. they do. The obvious attack is the timing, but the hidden step is 3: it only works if the merchants actually paid those premiums. Prephrase: the merchants weren’t really exposed to the insurers’ rates. Most students pick (B) because it is the author’s own criticism in the third paragraph, so it sounds like the passage’s official objection to Brandt. It fails because the author says that line of thought ‘would be compatible with Brandt’s central claim’; it changes why insurers preferred paid departments, not whether premiums drove the change. Attacking a point the account can absorb isn’t weakening it.

choices.note: Irrelevant. Fundraising for equipment fits with the volunteers being well equipped, which Brandt already says.

Tempting. This is the author’s own puzzle about Brandt. But the author says an answer to it ‘would be compatible with Brandt’s central claim.’ Whatever the insurers’ reasons, their premiums could still have driven the change.
It hints that paid departments did better, which might seem to back the standard view. But it’s about what happened after the change, not why the change was made.
Who later joined the paid departments says nothing about why the companies were disbanded.

CORRECT. If most merchants insured through societies whose rates ignored the kind of fire protection, the large insurers’ premiums gave them no financial reason to abolish their companies, and step 3 of Brandt’s chain fails.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?
choices: Ferreira rightly shows that suggestion can distort the Dolan test’s measures, but the problem calls for a reformed test rather than wholesale exclusion.
The Dolan test should be abandoned altogether, and every identification obtained through an unnecessarily suggestive procedure should be excluded from trial.
Ferreira’s critique of the Dolan test fails, because a witness’s stated certainty remains a dependable guide to the accuracy of an identification.
Because suggestion can distort a witness’s memory, an eyewitness identification should never by itself be sufficient to establish a defendant’s guilt.
Calvery’s courts have misapplied the Dolan test by giving too little weight to the witness’s opportunity to view the offender at the scene.
questions.explanation: The author accepts Ferreira’s diagnosis (“difficult to resist”) but argues that her remedy of exclusion is broader than needed and that a reformed test is the proportionate response, which is A. B is the trap: it is Ferreira’s conclusion, which the author resists; C contradicts the author’s acceptance of her diagnosis.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: State the author’s main point.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The first and third sentences of the third paragraph and the last sentence of the passage.

breakdown.analysis: Separate Ferreira from the author. Ferreira: the test defeats itself, so exclude. The author: her “diagnosis is difficult to resist,” but her “remedy sweeps more broadly than her diagnosis requires,” and in the last sentence, “a reformed test, not exclusion, is the proportionate response.” So: agree with the diagnosis, reject the remedy, propose reform. The trap will be Ferreira’s view dressed up as the main point.

choices.note: CORRECT. Accepts the diagnosis (“difficult to resist”), rejects the cure (“sweeps more broadly than her diagnosis requires”), and lands on the last sentence: a reformed test, not exclusion.
This is Ferreira’s conclusion, the very thing the author pushes back on (except, possibly, for single-suspect procedures). Another party’s view.
Contradicts the author, who accepts Ferreira’s diagnosis and says certainty on the stand tells a court more about later memory than about the identification.
Out of scope. The passage is about admitting identifications at trial, not about whether one can establish guilt on its own.
The passage never says courts underweight opportunity to view. The worry is that these factors can be inflated, not neglected.

questions.stem: According to the passage, under the rule announced in Regina v. Dolan, a judge who finds that an identification procedure was unnecessarily suggestive must
choices: exclude the resulting identification from trial unless the witness is willing to repeat it in court
instruct the jury to disregard any certainty the witness expresses about the identification
nonetheless admit the identification if, considering all of the circumstances, it appears to be reliable
require the police to conduct a second lineup that is entirely free of any suggestive features
admit the identification only if the witness had known the offender before the crime occurred
questions.explanation: The first paragraph says a judge who finds a procedure unnecessarily suggestive “must nonetheless admit the identification if, considering all the circumstances, it appears reliable,” which is C. A is the trap: exclusion is what Ferreira proposes, not what Dolan requires.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Recall what the Dolan rule requires.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The second sentence of the first paragraph.

breakdown.analysis: Straight detail. The first paragraph: a judge who finds a procedure unnecessarily suggestive “must nonetheless admit the identification if, considering all the circumstances, it appears reliable.” Look for that in synonyms. The likely trap is Ferreira’s rule (exclusion) dressed up as the law.

choices.note: Exclusion is Ferreira’s proposal, not Dolan’s rule, and the condition about repeating it in court appears nowhere. Under Dolan such identifications are “not automatically excluded.”
Nothing in Dolan says to tell juries anything. Certainty is one of the factors the judge weighs, not something to disregard.
CORRECT. Near-verbatim: “must nonetheless admit the identification if, considering all the circumstances, it appears reliable.”
Never mentioned. Dolan is about admitting or excluding, not redoing the lineup.
Borrows the author’s neighbor example from the third paragraph. Dolan has no prior-acquaintance requirement.

questions.stem: In calling the Dolan test “a thermometer that the fever itself can reset” (fourth sentence of the second paragraph), Ferreira most probably means that
choices: the test yields results that vary unpredictably from one judge to another, even when the facts are similar
judges’ own preconceptions about a defendant’s guilt distort the way in which they apply the test
the reliability factors grow less accurate simply because of the time that passes before trial
the measures the test uses to detect harm from suggestion can themselves be altered by the suggestion
the test detects the harm done by a suggestive procedure only when the suggestion was mild
questions.explanation: The metaphor sums up the second paragraph’s point: a suggestive procedure inflates the witness’s certainty and recalled view and attention, the very factors the court uses to check whether the suggestion did harm, which is D. C is tempting because the author later mentions months passing, but Ferreira’s point is that the suggestion, not time alone, changes the measures.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Decode the metaphor.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The second through fourth sentences of the second paragraph.

breakdown.analysis: Map the metaphor. Thermometer = the test (the reliability factors). Fever = the suggestion. Reset = the suggestion changes the readings. The sentence just before says it plainly: “A suggestive procedure can thus inflate the very measures a court consults to decide whether the suggestion did harm.” The instrument is changed by the very thing it’s supposed to measure.

choices.note: Nothing about judges disagreeing. The problem Ferreira describes would affect every judge the same way.
Wrong source of distortion. In the metaphor the fever, the suggestion, resets the thermometer, not the judge’s biases.
Tempting, because the author later mentions certainty “months after the procedure.” But Ferreira’s point is that the suggestion itself changes the measures. Time alone isn’t the fever.
CORRECT. The fever (suggestion) resets the thermometer (the reliability factors): the procedure inflates the very measures used to check it.
The metaphor says the test can be fooled, not that it works for mild suggestion. Indeed, “the worse the procedure, the more reliable the resulting identification may appear.”

questions.stem: The author mentions a witness who picks a longtime neighbor out of a fair lineup (third paragraph) primarily in order to
choices: show that suggestive procedures are sometimes necessary if the police are to identify an offender at all
give a case in which exclusion would discard an identification that is in all likelihood accurate
provide an example of a case in which a court of Calvery misapplied the factors listed in Dolan
suggest that witnesses who already know the offender are immune to the errors of memory Ferreira describes
illustrate how confirming feedback can inflate a witness’s confidence in an identification already made
questions.explanation: The example follows the claim that Ferreira’s remedy “sweeps more broadly than her diagnosis requires” and shows a case where exclusion would throw out a very likely accurate identification merely because a confirming remark followed it, which is B. D overstates “very likely accurate,” and E describes the second paragraph’s point.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Say why the neighbor example is there.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The third and fourth sentences of the third paragraph.

breakdown.analysis: Read the claim right before the example: Ferreira’s remedy “sweeps more broadly than her diagnosis requires.” Then: “Excluding every such identification would discard some that are very likely accurate,” followed by the neighbor. So the example is a case against the remedy: a witness who picks a longtime neighbor out of a fair lineup is almost surely right, and the only taint is a confirming remark afterward.

choices.note: Nothing in the example says the procedure was necessary. The lineup was fair; the suggestion came afterward, and the author never defends it.
CORRECT. The example illustrates the claim it’s attached to: excluding every such identification “would discard some that are very likely accurate.”
No court ruling is described. The example is a hypothetical aimed at Ferreira’s rule, not a misapplied Dolan case.
Too strong. The author calls the identification “very likely accurate,” not immune to memory error.
That’s the second paragraph’s point. Here the feedback is just what makes the identification excludable under Ferreira’s rule; it isn’t why the author mentions the case.

questions.stem: The author would be most likely to agree with which one of the following statements?
choices: Requiring police to record a witness’s initial confidence would remove the distorting effect of every kind of suggestive procedure.
Ferreira’s diagnosis applies with less force to witnesses who already knew the offender well before the crime occurred.
Identifications obtained by showing a witness a single suspect should continue to be judged by the Dolan factors as now measured.
A witness’s opportunity to view the offender has little bearing on whether the witness’s identification is accurate.
A witness’s certainty stated months later reveals less about an identification than confidence recorded at the moment of choice.
questions.explanation: In the third paragraph the author says certainty on the stand months later reflects what has happened to memory since more than the identification itself, and in the fourth proposes using confidence recorded at the first identification because it is fixed before feedback acts; the author would agree with E. B is the trap: the longtime-neighbor example shows that exclusion would discard identifications likely to be accurate, not that confirming feedback distorts such witnesses less; the author never says so. A ignores the conceded exception for showups, and C contradicts it.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find a claim the author would endorse, and check what each example in the passage is actually used to show.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The second and fourth sentences of the third paragraph (certainty on the stand; the longtime neighbor) and the fourth paragraph (the recorded-confidence proposal and its limits).

breakdown.analysis: Hard to prephrase, so collect the author’s commitments: 1. Ferreira’s diagnosis is right; 2. certainty stated on the stand reflects what happened to memory afterward; 3. a record made at the first identification, before feedback, avoids that contamination; 4. the fix won’t cure showups. Points 2 and 3 together rank the early record above later certainty. Most students pick (B) because of the neighbor example: surely a witness who knows the offender is less at risk? But look at what the author uses the example for: to show that blanket exclusion ‘would discard some [identifications] that are very likely accurate.’ The neighbor is still told she chose the suspect, so the feedback effect is still there. The author never says the diagnosis has less force for her. That’s an opinion the author never expressed.

choices.note: Too strong. The author concedes such a record ‘would not cure every suggestive procedure,’ naming single-suspect showups.

Tempting. The neighbor example makes it feel right. But the author uses that example to show that exclusion throws away likely-accurate identifications, and the neighbor still receives confirming feedback. Nothing says Ferreira’s diagnosis weakens for such witnesses.
Opposite. For showups, the author says Ferreira’s strictness ‘may well be warranted.’
At odds with the proposal: the author wants how well the witness saw the offender recorded early, which only makes sense if it matters.

CORRECT. Third paragraph: certainty stated months later tells more about what has happened to memory since than about the identification. Fourth paragraph: a record made at the first identification escapes that. The author ranks the early record above later certainty.

questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, would most seriously undermine the author’s proposal in the fourth paragraph?
choices: Witnesses who receive confirming feedback after an identification often recall having had a better view than they reported beforehand.
Jurors tend to give great weight to the testimony of eyewitnesses who express a high degree of certainty on the stand.
In ordinary lineups, officers who know which member is the suspect often signal it, unintentionally, while the witness is still choosing.
Recording a witness’s statement of confidence at the first identification takes little time and requires no special equipment.
A witness who is shown only a single suspect is steered toward that person before stating any confidence in the choice.
questions.explanation: The proposal works only if confidence recorded at the first identification is free of suggestion. C says suggestion commonly reaches witnesses during ordinary lineups, before any confidence is stated, so the record would be contaminated in the very cases the proposal is meant for. E is the trap: it describes a weakness of the record, but it is the one the author already concedes for showups, where Ferreira’s strictness ‘may well be warranted.’ A describes the post-identification feedback the proposal is designed to get around.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Attack the author’s proposal where it is meant to work.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The fourth paragraph (the proposal, its admitted limit for showups, and its stated target: ‘the distortion on which her critique chiefly rests’), with the second paragraph for that distortion.

breakdown.analysis: What does the proposal need? It says the record is ‘fixed before the confirming remarks Ferreira describes could act on it.’ That helps only if nothing suggestive reached the witness before the record was made. The author admits this fails for showups and carves them out. So what would really hurt? Suggestion arriving before the confidence statement in ordinary lineups, the cases the proposal is supposed to fix. Most students pick (E) because it plainly shows the record can be contaminated. It fails because the author already concedes exactly this for single-suspect procedures and limits the proposal to the other cases. Pointing out a limit the author has already admitted doesn’t undermine the argument.

choices.note: This is the post-identification feedback effect the proposal is designed to get around. If anything, it shows why the early record is needed.
This bears on why trial certainty matters, not on whether the early record is clean. If anything, it’s a reason to replace trial certainty with the record.

CORRECT. If officers commonly cue the witness during ordinary lineups before any confidence is stated, the early record is contaminated in the cases the proposal targets, and it loses its main advantage.
Makes the proposal easier to adopt. That helps it.

Tempting. It does show the record can be tainted. But the author concedes this for single-suspect showups (‘Admittedly…’) and says Ferreira may be right about them. The proposal is aimed at the other cases, so E leaves it standing.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?
choices: Tessel’s campion produces winged seeds chiefly to colonize newly opened ground, as botanists had long assumed, though more in meadows than on slopes.
Ferrel’s experiments with light have shown that Aldane was mistaken to attribute the campion’s pattern of seed production to competition among relatives.
The proportion of winged seeds a campion plant produces is an inherited trait that differs between the meadow and slope populations of the species.
Aldane’s sibling-competition account of the campion’s seed allocation has held up, though the light cue the plants rely on can mislead them.
Plants that produce two kinds of seed generally adjust the proportion of each to the quality of the light that reaches their leaves.
questions.explanation: The passage explains Aldane’s puzzling finding with her sibling-competition account, shows that the response is triggered by a red/far-red light cue, and ends by saying the account “has held up well” but that the cue can mislead, which is D. B is tempting, but Ferrel explains how the plants sense crowding, not why they respond; C contradicts the greenhouse result, and E overgeneralizes.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: State the main point.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The first sentence of the second paragraph and the last three sentences of the fourth paragraph.

breakdown.analysis: Map it. First paragraph: a puzzle (more winged seeds where open ground is scarce, not where it’s plentiful). Second: Aldane’s explanation, sibling competition, with a worked example. Third: the greenhouse shows the response is to conditions, not inherited. Fourth: Ferrel finds the cue (low red/far-red light), the cue can mislead, and the author says Aldane’s account “has held up well” with a refinement. We want: Aldane is basically right, plus the misleading-cue wrinkle.

choices.note: Contradicts the passage. The old colonization assumption is what Aldane’s survey puzzled; the passage explains the pattern by competition among siblings instead.
Tempting, since Ferrel’s work leads to a refinement. But the author says Aldane’s account “has held up well.” Ferrel explains how the plant senses crowding; he doesn’t overturn why it responds.
Contradicts the greenhouse result: the difference “was not inherited but a response to each plant’s conditions.”
CORRECT. Aldane’s account holds up; the refinement is that the plant tracks a light signal that usually, but not always, accompanies crowding.
Overgeneralizes from one species to all plants with two kinds of seed.

questions.stem: According to Aldane’s account as described in the second paragraph, plants on frequently disturbed slopes devote a smaller share of their seeds to the winged form than meadow plants do because on such slopes
choices: plants produce fewer seeds in total, so a smaller share of their seeds is lost to competition for gaps
heavy seeds that fall near the parent are likely to find room to establish rather than merely displacing siblings
the number of gaps that open in a season cannot be predicted from the density of the surrounding vegetation
a parent gains more descendants from each winged seed it produces than from each heavy seed it produces
winged seeds carried away from the parent compete mostly with the offspring of other plants rather than with siblings
questions.explanation: The last sentence of the second paragraph says that on a disturbed slope “open ground near the parent is plentiful, so heavy seeds dropped nearby are seldom wasted,” which is B. E is tempting because it repeats the passage’s words, but it is true of winged seeds in any habitat, so it cannot explain what is different about slopes; D describes the meadow case.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find Aldane’s reason for the slope plants’ smaller share of winged seeds.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The last sentence of the second paragraph.

breakdown.analysis: Aldane’s logic in the second paragraph: in a meadow, heavy seeds dropped nearby fight their siblings for a few gaps, so extra ones are wasted and winged seeds pay off. Then the last sentence: “On a disturbed slope the arithmetic is different: open ground near the parent is plentiful, so heavy seeds dropped nearby are seldom wasted.” That’s the reason. The trap will be a true statement about winged seeds that doesn’t say what’s different about slopes.

choices.note: The passage never compares total seed output on slopes and in meadows. It’s about shares, not totals.
CORRECT. Paraphrases the last sentence of the second paragraph: open ground near the parent is plentiful, so heavy seeds dropped nearby are seldom wasted.
Never said. The predictability of gaps plays no role in Aldane’s account.
This is the meadow situation, where winged seeds pay off. It would push slope plants toward more winged seeds, not fewer.
Tempting, because it uses the passage’s own words. But that’s true of winged seeds anywhere, so it can’t explain what’s different about slopes.

questions.stem: According to the passage, Aldane’s greenhouse experiment showed that
choices: plants with meadow parents produced a higher proportion of winged seeds than plants with slope parents at either density
a low ratio of red to far-red light by itself sufficed to raise the proportion of winged seeds a plant produced
plants grown at high density produced fewer seeds in total than did plants of the same origin grown at low density
the proportion of winged seeds a plant produced depended both on how densely it was grown and on its parents’ habitat
the proportion of winged seeds a plant produced depended on how densely it was grown, not on its parents’ habitat
questions.explanation: The third paragraph says crowded plants produced a high proportion of winged seeds and sparse plants a low one “regardless of whether their parents had come from meadow or slope,” which is E. B is the trap: it is true according to the passage, but it was Ferrel’s finding, not Aldane’s. A and D contradict “regardless.”

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Recall what the greenhouse experiment found.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The second through fourth sentences of the third paragraph.

breakdown.analysis: The third paragraph: crowded plants made a high proportion of winged seeds, sparse plants a low one, “regardless of whether their parents had come from meadow or slope.” So density mattered and parental habitat didn’t. Watch for two traps: a true finding from the wrong experiment, and answers that sneak parental habitat back in.

choices.note: Contradicts “regardless of whether their parents had come from meadow or slope.”
Tempting, because the passage does say this. But it was Ferrel’s 2010 lamp experiment, not Aldane’s greenhouse. Right fact, wrong study.
Total seed output is never mentioned. The experiment measured the proportion of winged seeds.
Half right. Density mattered, but the “regardless” clause rules out parental habitat.
CORRECT. Density drove the proportion; parental habitat didn’t (“regardless of whether their parents had come from meadow or slope”).

questions.stem: The author discusses a parent that drops forty heavy seeds where two gaps open (second paragraph) primarily in order to
choices: illustrate why, in crowded conditions, more seeds dropped beside the parent add little to its descendants
estimate the number of gaps that typically open around a campion plant in a meadow in one season
show that heavy seeds are less likely than winged seeds to germinate in a gap in the turf
explain why plants on frequently disturbed slopes produce fewer seeds in total than plants in valley meadows
suggest that winged seeds seldom travel far enough from the parent to escape competition with their siblings
questions.explanation: The forty-seeds example is a worked illustration of Aldane’s logic: only as many seeds as there are gaps can establish nearby, so extra heavy seeds are simply lost, which is A. B is tempting because the example uses numbers, but it begins with “Suppose” and is hypothetical; E reverses the point about winged seeds.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Say why the forty-seed example is there.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The second and third sentences of the second paragraph.

breakdown.analysis: The example follows the claim that a seed dropped beside its parent competes for a few gaps, mostly with its siblings. Forty seeds, two gaps: at most two establish, the rest are lost. So piling more seeds beside the parent buys nothing. That sets up why winged seeds pay off in meadows. It illustrates a mechanism; it doesn’t report data.

choices.note: CORRECT. Forty seeds, two gaps, at most two establish: in a crowded meadow, adding seeds beside the parent does little to add descendants.
Tempting because of the numbers, but the example starts with “Suppose.” It’s hypothetical, not a field estimate.
The example is about how many seeds can establish, not about how well each kind of seed germinates.
Total seed output is never discussed, and the example concerns a crowded meadow, not a slope.
Reverses the point. Winged seeds are said to escape sibling competition, competing “mostly with the offspring of other plants.”

questions.stem: The author’s attitude toward Aldane’s explanation of the campion’s seed allocation can most accurately be described as
choices: skeptical, because her greenhouse experiment could not separate inherited differences from responses to each plant’s conditions
neutral, since the author reports her findings and Ferrel’s without evaluating the merits of either
dismissive, because Ferrel later showed that light quality, rather than competition, governs how the plants allocate seed
wholly approving, since later work has confirmed every element of the explanation she originally offered
largely favorable, though the author suggests the plants track a signal of crowding rather than crowding itself
questions.explanation: In the fourth paragraph the author says Aldane’s account “has held up well” but suggests a refinement: the plant responds to a signal that ordinarily accompanies crowding rather than to crowding itself, which is E. D is too strong, since the author proposes a refinement; C confuses the trigger (light) with the reason the response exists (competition).

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Pin down the author’s attitude toward Aldane’s account.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The second-to-last sentence of the fourth paragraph.

breakdown.analysis: The author’s verdict is explicit: Aldane’s account “has held up well, but such cases suggest a refinement.” Positive, with a qualification. The refinement: the plant responds “not to crowding itself but to a signal that ordinarily accompanies crowding.” We need favorable, with that reservation. Attitude traps overshoot in both directions.

choices.note: Contradicts the passage. The greenhouse experiment is exactly what separated inherited differences from responses to conditions.
The author does evaluate: the account “has held up well.” Not neutral.
Confuses the trigger (light) with the reason the response exists (sibling competition). Ferrel explains how the plant senses crowding; he doesn’t replace Aldane’s why.
Too strong. The author proposes a refinement and notes that the cue can mislead the plant.
CORRECT. “Has held up well” = largely favorable; the reservation is that the plant tracks a signal that ordinarily accompanies crowding.

questions.stem: The information in the passage most strongly supports which one of the following about the plants grown at high density in Aldane’s greenhouse experiment?
choices: They produced a high proportion of winged seeds because their neighbors reduced the overall amount of light reaching their leaves.
They produced more winged seeds in absolute number than did the plants that were grown at low density.
Their neighbors probably altered the composition, and not merely the amount, of the light that reached their leaves.
Those with slope parents produced a lower proportion of winged seeds than those with meadow parents.
Their winged seeds would have been less likely to reach open gaps than those of the plants grown sparsely.
questions.explanation: Crowded plants made a high proportion of winged seeds (third paragraph), and Ferrel showed that the plants sense crowding through light that has passed through or bounced off neighboring leaves and so is poor in red relative to far-red (fourth paragraph). The crowded plants’ light was therefore probably changed in its makeup, C.
