A is the trap: it swaps the ratio for the amount, but Ferrel found that ‘merely dimming the lamps had no effect.’ B confuses a proportion with a number; D contradicts ‘regardless.’

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Combine the greenhouse result with Ferrel’s light mechanism.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The third paragraph (crowded vs. sparse pots) and the first three sentences of the fourth paragraph (red, far-red, and dimming).

breakdown.analysis: Put two paragraphs together. Third: crowded pots → high proportion of winged seeds. Fourth: light that has passed through or bounced off leaves is poor in red relative to far-red, and that ratio alone triggers winged seeds; dimming alone does nothing. Crowded pots mean lots of neighboring foliage, so the crowded plants probably got light with less red in the mix. The key never says ‘red’ or ‘far-red’; it says ‘composition,’ which is the ratio in other words. Most students pick (A) because it’s the obvious picture: neighbors shade you. It fails on one word: Ferrel found the trigger is the kind of light, not the amount (‘merely dimming the lamps had no effect’).

choices.note: Tempting. Shading is the obvious effect of neighbors. But Ferrel found that ‘merely dimming the lamps had no effect’; the trigger is the red/far-red ratio, not the amount of light.
Confuses a proportion with a number. The passage gives proportions only and nothing about total seed output.

CORRECT. Neighbors’ leaves absorb red and pass far-red, so light reaching a crowded plant is changed in its makeup. ‘Composition’ is the ratio; ‘not merely the amount’ keeps the claim clear of the dimming result. ‘Probably’ is the right strength.
Contradicts the greenhouse result: parental habitat didn’t matter (‘regardless of whether their parents had come from meadow or slope’).
Nothing in a greenhouse experiment tells us where seeds would land. Speculation.

questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, would most call into question the author’s suggestion (fourth paragraph) that the seed allocation of campion growing beneath birch may serve those plants poorly?
choices: Heavy seeds that fall beneath young birch germinate about as readily as heavy seeds that fall on open ground elsewhere on the slopes.
Campion growing beneath birch produce fewer seeds in total than do campion growing in the open on the same slopes.
Winged seeds produced by meadow plants are more likely to reach a gap than winged seeds produced by birch-shaded plants.
Seedlings that establish beneath young birch seldom survive long enough to flower, because the shade deepens as the trees mature.
Campion from open slopes that are grown under light filtered through birch leaves produce winged seeds in meadow proportions.
questions.explanation: The author suspects that birch-shaded plants waste effort on winged seeds, because open ground beneath them would let heavy seeds establish nearby. D shows that seedlings near the parent seldom survive to flower, so sending seeds away is actually the better strategy there and the allocation may serve the plant well. E is the trap: it confirms that birch-filtered light triggers the meadow response, which the author already says, but says nothing about whether the response helps or hurts. A supports the author, B concerns total output, and C points the wrong way.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Weaken the claim that the birch-shaded plants’ seed allocation may hurt them.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The last four sentences of the fourth paragraph (‘Yet the cue is imperfect…’ through ‘…has yet to be measured’).

breakdown.analysis: Why does the author think the birch-shaded plants may be misled? Open ground below means heavy seeds dropped nearby could establish, so making lots of winged seeds looks wasteful. That quietly assumes nearby seedlings would do well. So what if open ground near the parent is a dead end? Then sending seeds away is smart. Prephrase: something makes the spot beneath the birch bad for seedlings. Most students pick (E) because it’s a neat experimental confirmation about birch light. It fails because it confirms what the author already grants (the cue fires under birch) and says nothing about cost or benefit. Corroborating a premise isn’t touching the conclusion.

choices.note: Wrong direction. If heavy seeds do fine beneath birch, dropping them nearby would work, which makes the winged-seed allocation look more wasteful. That supports the author.
Total output isn’t the issue. The suggestion is about the split between winged and heavy seeds.
If anything, this makes winged seeds look like a worse bet for birch-shaded plants, which supports the author’s suggestion.

CORRECT. If seedlings beneath the birch seldom live to flower, heavy seeds dropped there are effectively wasted, and dispersing seeds away is the better strategy. The ‘misled’ allocation may then serve the plant well.
Tempting. It neatly confirms that birch-filtered light triggers the meadow response. But the author already says so; whether that response helps or hurts the plant is untouched.

questions.stimulus: Growers in the Taln Valley have noticed something surprising. Apples whose skins develop russeting, a rough brown patch, are generally regarded as blemished, and they fetch lower prices at market. Yet when stored through the winter, russeted apples usually stay free of rot considerably longer than smooth-skinned apples picked from the same trees.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to explain the growers' observation?
choices: Russeted apples are usually sold to cider makers, who pay less for fruit than grocery chains do.
Some apple varieties grown in the Taln Valley never develop russeting, whatever the weather in a given season.
Shoppers generally choose smooth-skinned apples over russeted ones even when the two are offered at the same price.
The corky layer of a russet patch also slows the entry of fungi that rot apples.
Russeting is most common in wet springs, and wet weather also encourages the fungi that cause stored apples to rot.
questions.explanation: The puzzle is why a supposed blemish goes with fruit that keeps better; D explains it by showing that the russet layer itself protects the apple from rot. E is the trap: it ties russeting to wet weather, which favors rot, so it makes the observation more puzzling rather than less.

setup.label: Paradox
setup.text: Russeting is treated as a blemish, but russeted apples resist rot in storage longer than smooth ones.

breakdown.analysis: How can a blemish go along with a better-keeping apple? This is the classic paradox engine: the defect turns out to help. Russeting is bad for how an apple looks and sells, but that doesn't mean it's bad for the apple. We need an answer that shows the russet patch somehow protects the fruit.

choices.note: So? Who buys russeted apples and what they pay explains the lower price, not why the apples resist rot.
Irrelevant. Apples that never russet aren't part of the comparison between russeted and smooth fruit from the same trees.
Shopper taste is the wrong dimension. It explains why russeted apples are seen as blemished, not why they keep longer.
CORRECT. The same change that makes the skin look blemished shields the fruit from rot. A defect in looks, a benefit in storage. Both facts now fit.
Opposite direction. If russeting goes with wet weather, and wet weather favors rot, we'd expect russeted apples to rot sooner. This deepens the puzzle.

questions.stimulus:
Marisol: The city arts council should stop giving grants to the Brindle Street Theater. Its shows sell out every night, so its ticket sales obviously cover its costs, and grant money should go to companies that cannot pay their own way.

Teodor: Selling out does not mean the Brindle covers its costs. Its auditorium holds only ninety seats, and it deliberately keeps ticket prices low. Without the grant, it would have to raise prices sharply, pricing out many of its regular patrons.
questions.stem: Marisol and Teodor disagree over whether
choices: the Brindle Street Theater's ticket sales alone bring in enough money to cover all of the theater's costs
grant money should go to theater companies that cannot pay their own way through ticket sales
the Brindle Street Theater's productions are popular enough to fill its auditorium every night
a theater company that receives an arts council grant should be expected to keep its ticket prices low
the arts council's grants are what has allowed the Brindle Street Theater to sell out its shows
questions.explanation: Marisol says the sold-out shows mean ticket sales obviously cover the Brindle's costs; Teodor flatly denies that, so A is the point at issue. D is tempting because Teodor values low prices, but Marisol says nothing about ticket prices, so there is no disagreement there.

setup.label: Arguments
setup.text: Marisol: The Brindle sells out, so its ticket sales cover its costs; grants should go to companies that can't pay their way. Teodor: Selling out doesn't mean it covers its costs; with only ninety seats and low prices, it needs the grant.

breakdown.analysis: To disagree, one speaker must say yes and the other no. Marisol: ticket sales cover costs, yes. Teodor's first sentence: no, they don't. That's the clash. Notice what Teodor doesn't attack: Marisol's principle that grants should go to companies that can't pay their way. He may well accept it; he just thinks the Brindle is one of those companies.

choices.note: CORRECT. Marisol: yes, ticket sales obviously cover its costs. Teodor: selling out does not mean it covers its costs. Direct yes/no.
Tempting, but Teodor never rejects this principle. His point is that the Brindle can't pay its way, which fits the principle. No disagreement.
Both agree. Marisol says it sells out every night; Teodor accepts that and argues from it.
Tempting, since Teodor cares about keeping prices low. But Marisol says nothing about ticket prices. One speaker silent means no disagreement we can confirm.
Neither speaker commits to this. Marisol never discusses why the shows sell out, and Teodor talks about what would happen without the grant, not about what caused past sell-outs.

questions.stimulus: Dog owner: Veterinarians routinely urge owners to have their dogs' teeth professionally cleaned every year to prevent gum disease. But my terrier, Biscuit, lived to the age of fifteen without a single cleaning, and his gums stayed healthy to the end. Clearly, the risk that gum disease poses to dogs whose teeth are never cleaned has been greatly exaggerated.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the dog owner's argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument
choices: attacks the motives of veterinarians rather than addressing the evidence that supports their recommendation of annual cleanings
presumes, without providing justification, that annual cleanings are the only way to prevent gum disease in dogs
infers a general conclusion about dogs from a single case that may not be typical
fails to consider that some dogs whose teeth are cleaned every year nonetheless develop gum disease
takes for granted that a recommendation made by most experts in a field must be correct
questions.explanation: One healthy terrier tells us almost nothing about how often uncleaned teeth lead to gum disease in dogs generally, so C names the flaw. A is tempting because the owner is disagreeing with veterinarians, but the owner never questions their motives; the problem is the evidence, not an attack on the source.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The risk of gum disease for dogs whose teeth are never cleaned has been greatly exaggerated.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Biscuit never had a cleaning and his gums stayed healthy for fifteen years.

breakdown.analysis: So what if Biscuit was fine? One dog is one dog. Structure: 1. Vets say annual cleanings prevent gum disease. 2. Biscuit had no cleanings and no gum disease. So the risk is exaggerated. That's the anecdote-versus-general-claim flaw; it's a classic, know it. It's like saying: my uncle smoked and lived to 90, so the risks of smoking are exaggerated. We need an answer that says the owner generalizes from one possibly lucky case.

choices.note: Tempting, because the owner is pushing back on veterinarians. But the owner never says vets have bad motives (like wanting to sell cleanings). No attack on motives happens here.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Vets only recommend yearly cleanings because they get paid for them, so we can ignore the advice.

choices.note: The owner never claims cleanings are the only prevention. The owner claims the risk without cleanings is small. Different claim.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Since Biscuit wasn't cleaned, he must have gotten gum disease, because cleaning is the only way to prevent it.

choices.note: CORRECT. The whole argument rests on one dog. Biscuit might have had unusually good genes or diet. A single case can't show what usually happens to dogs.
Irrelevant. If cleaned dogs sometimes get gum disease anyway, that would, if anything, help the owner. It isn't something the argument needed to consider.
choices.example: Example of a real failure to consider: Cleaned dogs rarely get gum disease, so cleaning prevents it (ignoring that owners who pay for cleanings may also feed better diets).

choices.note: Backwards. The owner rejects the experts' recommendation; he certainly doesn't assume they must be right.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Most vets recommend yearly cleanings, so yearly cleanings must be necessary.

questions.stimulus: Last year the Quenby water utility began phoning customers in its northern district with an estimated completion time whenever their water service is shut off for repairs. Since then, complaints from northern-district customers about service interruptions have fallen by half, even though interruptions there have been as frequent and as long as before. So the calls, by telling customers what to expect, have made interruptions less frustrating.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the argument?
choices: Customers in the northern district complain far more often about their water bills than about interruptions in service.
The phone calls cost the utility less to make than it had originally projected when it planned the program.
In the utility's southern district, where customers received no such calls, complaints about interruptions did not decline.
Some customers in the northern district say that they usually hang up before hearing the estimated completion time.
Water service interruptions in the northern district are, on average, shorter than those in the utility's southern district.
questions.explanation: The argument credits the calls for the drop in complaints, so an answer that rules out a utility-wide cause helps; C shows that the district without calls saw no such drop. E is tempting because it is about interruptions, but it compares the two districts at one time and says nothing about why complaints in the northern district changed.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The phone calls made service interruptions less frustrating for northern-district customers.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: After the calls began, interruption complaints in the northern district fell by half; interruptions were as frequent and as long as before.

breakdown.analysis: Complaints dropped after the calls began. But was it the calls? Maybe complaints dropped everywhere, say because the utility made complaining harder or a new billing system put customers in a better mood. To strengthen a before-and-after causal claim, rule out other causes. We need an answer that says complaints didn't fall where there were no calls.

choices.note: Wrong topic. Billing complaints don't tell us why interruption complaints fell.
Wrong dimension. What the calls cost has nothing to do with whether they reduced frustration.
CORRECT. This is the comparison group. The district without calls saw no drop, so a utility-wide cause is less likely and the calls look like the difference.
This slightly weakens the argument: a call nobody listens to can't calm anybody. Wrong direction.

Tempting, since it's about interruptions. But it's a snapshot comparison between districts. The argument is about a change in the northern district over time, and we already know its interruptions didn't change.

questions.stimulus: Only about 12 percent of Dunmere's registered voters cast ballots in last May's election for the town water board, whereas more than 60 percent voted in last November's election for mayor. So if the water-board election were moved to November and placed on the same ballot as the mayor's race, far more voters would help choose the water board's members.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the argument?
choices: Most voters who take part in November elections are already well informed about the water board's responsibilities.
A substantial number of those who vote in November would not leave the water-board race blank.
Turnout in Dunmere's November elections will be at least as high in future years as it was last year.
Everyone who voted in last May's water-board election would also cast a ballot in a November election.
Moving the water-board election to November would not increase the overall cost of running Dunmere's town elections.
questions.explanation: Showing up to vote is not the same as voting in every race on the ballot; the argument needs B, that many November voters would actually mark a choice for water board. Negate it (nearly all leave it blank) and the plan adds no voters. C is the too-strong trap: turnout could dip a little from 60 percent and still dwarf 12 percent.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Moving the water-board race to the November ballot would mean far more voters help choose the board.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: May water-board turnout was about 12 percent; November mayoral turnout was over 60 percent.

breakdown.analysis: More people would hold the ballot. But would they vote in the water-board race? People who come out for mayor might skip the obscure races further down. The argument quietly treats 'cast a ballot' as 'voted in every race'. We need an answer that says enough November voters would actually fill in the water-board line.

choices.note: Not required. Voters don't have to be well informed to cast a vote. Negated, the argument still stands.
choices.negation: It is not the case that most November voters are well informed about the water board. (They can still vote in the race.)

choices.note: CORRECT. Negate it and almost every November voter leaves the water-board race blank. Then turnout for the ballot rises but participation in the water-board choice doesn't. The argument collapses.
choices.negation: Almost none of the November voters would mark a choice in the water-board race.

choices.note: Tempting, but too strong. Turnout could fall to 50 percent and still crush 12 percent. The argument survives the negation.
choices.negation: Turnout in future November elections will be somewhat lower than last year's. (Still far above 12 percent.)

choices.note: Too strong. If a few May voters skipped November, the total could still rise enormously.
choices.negation: At least one person who voted in May would not vote in November. (Doesn't matter given the size of the gap.)

choices.note: Wrong dimension. The conclusion is about how many people vote, not about cost.
choices.negation: Moving the election would increase the cost of running elections. (More voters could still take part.)

questions.stimulus: Conservator: Many museums now remove the overpaint that earlier restorers added to old paintings, on the grounds that it is not the original artist's work. Yet some overpaint is itself centuries old and records how later generations understood the painting. Removing it destroys historical evidence that can never be recovered. So, although overpaint that hides or harms original paint may need to come off, a museum should not remove old overpaint merely because the original artist did not apply it.
questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the overall conclusion drawn in the conservator's argument?
choices: Removing overpaint from old paintings destroys historical evidence that, once lost, can never be recovered.
Overpaint that hides or harms a painting's original paint should be removed, whatever its age or origin.
Many museums now remove the overpaint that earlier restorers added to old paintings, because it is not the artist's work.
Some overpaint is centuries old and records how later generations understood the paintings to which it was added.
Old overpaint should not be removed from a painting merely because the original artist did not apply it.
questions.explanation: Everything builds to the last clause: old overpaint should not be removed merely because the artist didn't apply it, which E restates. A is the tempting trap; it is a premise supporting that conclusion, and the claim about overpaint that hides or harms original paint is only the conservator's concession.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: A museum should not remove old overpaint merely because the original artist didn't apply it.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Some overpaint is centuries old and records later understanding; removing it destroys unrecoverable evidence.

breakdown.analysis: Ask which statement supports which. The conclusion is the one everything else supports. Sentence 1 is background (what museums do and why). Sentences 2 and 3 are reasons. The last sentence opens with a concession ('although ... may need to come off') and then gives the claim the reasons were for. That final 'should not remove ... merely because' is the conclusion.

choices.note: Tempting, because it's the strongest-sounding claim. But it's a reason given for the conclusion, not the conclusion itself. Ask: does this support the 'should not' claim? Yes. So it's a premise.
This is the concession, and overstated. The conservator grants only that such overpaint 'may need to come off'; it isn't what the argument is trying to prove.
Background. It sets up the practice the conservator is responding to.
A premise. It supports the claim that removal destroys evidence.
CORRECT. This is the final claim, minus the concession: old overpaint shouldn't come off just because someone other than the artist applied it.

questions.stimulus: Many gardeners believe that watering plants in bright midday sun scorches their leaves, because the water droplets focus sunlight like tiny magnifying glasses. In controlled trials, however, droplets on most leaves either spread flat or evaporated before they could focus enough light to do harm. Scorching occurred only on a few species with hairy leaves, whose hairs hold droplets up above the leaf surface. Thus, ______.
questions.stem: Which one of the following most logically completes the argument?
choices: the belief that midday watering scorches leaves holds true for far fewer kinds of plants than many gardeners suppose
water droplets cannot focus sunlight strongly enough to scorch the leaves of any plant in an ordinary garden
gardeners would be wise to avoid watering their plants in bright midday sun, whatever species they happen to grow
plants with hairy leaves suffer more damage from strong midday sun than smooth-leaved plants do, whether or not they are watered
the controlled trials did not reproduce the conditions under which most gardeners actually water their plants
questions.explanation: The trials show the scorching effect is real but limited to a few hairy-leaved species, so the popular belief holds for far fewer plants than gardeners think, which is A. C is the trap: it repeats the popular advice that the author is pushing back against, even though the evidence shows midday watering is harmless for most plants.

setup.label: Facts
setup.text: 1. Many gardeners think midday watering scorches leaves because droplets focus sunlight; 2. in trials, droplets on most leaves spread flat or evaporated before doing harm; 3. scorching happened only on a few hairy-leaved species.

breakdown.analysis: Where is the author going? The first sentence is the popular view. The 'however' signals pushback: on most leaves, nothing happens. But the author also concedes a real effect on a few hairy-leaved plants. So the conclusion should be qualified: the belief isn't baseless, but it covers far fewer plants than people think. Watch for answers that repeat the popular view or swing to the opposite extreme ('never').

choices.note: CORRECT. It keeps both halves: the effect is real (hairy-leaved species) but narrow (most leaves are fine). That's exactly where the evidence points.
Too strong. The trials found scorching on a few hairy-leaved species, so 'any plant' contradicts the evidence.
Tempting, because it sounds like sensible caution. But it's the popular view the author is arguing against. For most species the trials found no harm, so 'whatever species' runs the wrong way.
We don't know this. The hairy-leaved plants were scorched because they held droplets up. Nothing is said about sun damage without water.
Unsupported, and it cuts against the author. The argument uses the trials as good evidence; nothing suggests they were unrealistic.

questions.stimulus: Veterinarian: The Tulls' elderly cat has a tumor that could be surgically removed. But the cat would face several weeks of painful recovery, and even with the surgery it would probably live only a few months longer than it would without it. So although the Tulls could easily afford the operation, I advised them against it.
questions.stem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the veterinarian's reasoning?
choices: A veterinarian should advise against any treatment that an animal's owners would not be able to afford easily.
Whether an animal undergoes surgery should be decided by the animal's owners rather than by its veterinarian.
A veterinarian should recommend surgery whenever the surgery is likely to extend the animal's life by any amount.
A veterinarian should advise against surgery that would bring a painful recovery and likely add only a few months of life.
A veterinarian should advise against surgery for an animal only if the animal is unlikely to survive the operation itself.
questions.explanation: The vet's reasons are a painful recovery and only a few extra months of life, and D says exactly those two facts call for advising against surgery. E is tempting because it is about when to advise against surgery, but it would forbid this advice, since nothing suggests the cat would not survive the operation.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The veterinarian was right to advise the Tulls against the surgery.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Recovery would be painful for weeks; the surgery would probably add only a few months of life; cost is not an issue.

breakdown.analysis: A principle-justify answer has to tell you to do what the conclusion says, using the facts you're given. The facts: painful recovery, little extra life, money no problem. The action: advise against surgery. We need a rule like: if recovery is painful and the gain in life is small, advise against.

choices.note: Wrong facts. The Tulls can easily afford it, so this rule doesn't apply and gives no support.
Doesn't justify the advice. Owners deciding is consistent with a vet giving advice either way.
Opposite. Surgery would extend life a little, so this rule would call for recommending it.
CORRECT. Both conditions match: painful recovery, and no more than a few months gained. The rule then says advise against, which is what the vet did.
Tempting, since it's about advising against surgery. But 'only if' makes survival risk a requirement, and nothing says the cat might not survive. So this rule would actually condemn the advice.

questions.stimulus: In a recent study, people who described themselves as habitual procrastinators kept a daily diary for a month, noting each task they put off and how they felt each evening. On 70 percent of the days on which they put off an important task, they reported feeling anxious that evening. This shows that putting off important tasks tends to make habitual procrastinators anxious.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the argument is flawed in that the argument
choices: draws a conclusion about people in general from a study limited to those who call themselves habitual procrastinators
fails to consider how often the participants felt anxious on days when they put off nothing important
takes for granted that the participants put off unimportant tasks less often than they put off important ones
confuses a condition that is necessary for feeling anxious with a condition that is sufficient for it
presumes, without providing justification, that the participants were right to describe themselves as habitual procrastinators
questions.explanation: Seventy percent means nothing without a baseline: if the participants felt anxious on 70 percent of all their evenings, procrastinating made no difference, so B names the missing comparison. A is tempting but misreads the conclusion, which is limited to habitual procrastinators, the very group studied.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Putting off important tasks tends to make habitual procrastinators anxious.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: On 70 percent of the days they put off an important task, participants reported anxiety that evening.

breakdown.analysis: Seventy percent sounds high. High compared to what? If these people feel anxious on 70 percent of all evenings, procrastination changes nothing. This is the missing comparison group: the study reports what happened on procrastination days only. It's like saying a lucky sweater works because your team won 70 percent of the games you wore it, without checking how often they win when you don't. We need an answer that points to the non-procrastination days.

choices.note: Tempting at a glance, but read the conclusion: it's about habitual procrastinators only, the same group studied. No leap to people in general.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Habitual procrastinators get anxious when they delay tasks, so everyone does.

choices.note: CORRECT. Without the anxiety rate on other days, 70 percent has no baseline. If they're anxious 70 percent of the time anyway, procrastinating makes no difference.
Irrelevant. Unimportant tasks never enter the argument, and nothing depends on how often they're delayed.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Since procrastinators delay important tasks, they must delay trivial ones even more.

choices.note: No conditional confusion here. The argument never treats procrastination as required for anxiety or as guaranteeing it.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Anyone who procrastinates gets anxious, so anyone anxious must have procrastinated.

choices.note: So? If a few participants weren't 'true' procrastinators, the core problem remains. This is a nitpick about labels, not the gap.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Our survey respondents call themselves early risers, so they must wake before six.

questions.stimulus: Councilor: Some residents propose that only people who have lived in Fairhaven for at least ten years be allowed to serve on its planning commission, on the grounds that long residence ensures familiarity with the town's needs. But under that rule, the engineer who designed Fairhaven's flood-control system, who moved here six years ago and knows the town's drainage better than anyone, would be barred from serving. Clearly, length of residence is a poor test of familiarity with the town's needs.
questions.stem: The claim that the engineer who designed Fairhaven's flood-control system would be barred from serving plays which one of the following roles in the councilor's argument?
choices: It is the conclusion that the councilor's argument as a whole is designed to establish.
It is a premise that the residents offer in support of their proposal for the commission.
It is a general principle from which the councilor derives the claim about length of residence.
It is offered as evidence that the residents' proposal would be difficult to enforce in practice.
It is presented as an unacceptable consequence of adopting the criterion that the residents propose.
questions.explanation: The councilor shows that the ten-year rule would exclude the person who arguably knows the town's needs best and uses that bad result to reject the rule's premise, so E is right. D is tempting because the claim is aimed against the proposal, but the councilor's point is that the rule gives the wrong answer, not that it is hard to enforce.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Length of residence is a poor test of familiarity with Fairhaven's needs.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Under the ten-year rule, the flood-control engineer, who knows the town's drainage best, would be barred.

breakdown.analysis: The councilor takes the residents' rule, applies it, and gets a result that looks absurd: the person who knows the drainage best can't serve. The councilor doesn't like this outcome. It's the absurd result used to sink the rule. The claim supports the conclusion, so it's a premise, but a specific kind: a consequence the councilor rejects.

choices.note: No. The conclusion is the last sentence, about residence being a poor test. The engineer example supports it.
Opposite. The example is aimed against the residents' proposal, not for it.
It's a specific case, not a general principle.

Tempting, because the example does count against the proposal. But it's about the rule giving a bad result, not about enforcement. Nothing suggests the rule would be hard to apply; it applies all too easily.
CORRECT. The councilor derives the engineer's exclusion from the proposed criterion and treats that outcome as unacceptable, which discredits the criterion.

questions.stimulus: The striped blenny, a small reef fish, often bobs its head rapidly when another blenny approaches. Male blennies do this far more often than females do, and only males defend territories on the reef. So the head-bobbing is probably a warning that males use to drive rivals away from their territories.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the argument?
choices: Male blennies that lose their territories to rivals stop bobbing their heads within a few days of the loss.
Several other reef fish species defend their territories without making any head movements at all.
Male blennies bob their heads far more often when a female approaches than when a male does.
Head-bobbing is common among many other species of small fish found on the same reefs.
Blennies bob their heads more rapidly in warm water than they do in cooler water.
questions.explanation: If males bob mostly at approaching females, the display looks like courtship rather than a warning to rivals, so C undercuts the proposed function. A is tempting because it ties bobbing to territory, but that link supports the argument rather than weakening it.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Head-bobbing is probably a male's warning to drive rivals from his territory.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Blennies bob when another approaches; males bob far more than females; only males hold territories.

breakdown.analysis: The argument guesses a function from who does it. But males do lots of things females don't, like courting. Maybe the bob is about attracting mates, not repelling rivals. When an argument guesses what a trait is for, weaken it with a different job the trait could be doing. We need an answer that points to another function, ideally tied to who the bob is aimed at.

choices.note: Tempting, since it mentions territory. But it strengthens the argument: no territory, no bobbing, which fits a territorial warning. Wrong direction.
So? Other species defending territories some other way says nothing about what this blenny's bob is for.
CORRECT. If males bob mostly at females, the bob looks like a courtship signal. A warning to rivals should be aimed at rival males.
Irrelevant. That many fish bob doesn't tell us what blennies bob for.
Irrelevant. Water temperature affecting speed says nothing about the bob's purpose.

questions.stimulus: Under Penner Marina's rules, a boat may leave the marina only if its bilge pump has been tested that same day, and a bilge pump may be tested only by a staff member who holds a current safety certificate. Any boat carrying paying passengers must also have a licensed pilot aboard, unless it is a water taxi running to Gull Island. Today every boat obeyed these rules, and the Wren, which is carrying paying passengers and is not a water taxi, left the marina.
questions.stem: If the statements above are true, which one of the following must also be true?
choices: Today the Wren's bilge pump was tested by a staff member who holds a current safety certificate.
The licensed pilot aboard the Wren today holds a current safety certificate from the marina.
Every boat that left Penner Marina today, whether or not it carried passengers, had a licensed pilot aboard.
Any boat whose bilge pump is tested today by a certified staff member may leave the marina.
No water taxi running between the marina and Gull Island carried paying passengers today.
questions.explanation: The Wren left, so its bilge pump was tested today, and only certified staff may test pumps, so A must be true. D is the reversal trap: the rules make a test necessary for leaving, not sufficient.

setup.label: Facts
setup.text: 1. Leaves marina → pump tested that day; 2. Pump tested → by a certified staff member; 3. Paying passengers AND not a water taxi → licensed pilot aboard; 4. The rules were obeyed today; 5. The Wren carried paying passengers, isn't a water taxi, and left.

breakdown.analysis: Chain it: Wren left → pump tested today → tester was certified. That's the main chain. Separately, the Wren had paying passengers and isn't a water taxi → it had a licensed pilot. Watch for answers that reverse an arrow or apply a rule to boats we know nothing about.

choices.note: CORRECT. Left → tested today → tested by a certified staff member. Both links are in the rules, and the rules were obeyed.
We don't know this. The Wren had a pilot, but nothing says the pilot did the test or holds a certificate.
Too broad. Water taxis and boats without paying passengers don't need pilots, and some of those may have left today.
This reverses the rule. A test is required for leaving ('only if'), not a guarantee of it. Other rules, like the pilot rule, could still keep a boat in.
We don't know. Water taxis are just exempt from the pilot rule; nothing says whether any carried passengers.

questions.stimulus: Surveys in the city of Tolland show that residents of neighborhoods with a full-service grocery store eat considerably more fresh fruit and vegetables than residents of neighborhoods without one. Yet when new full-service grocery stores opened in several Tolland neighborhoods that had lacked them, residents' consumption of fruit and vegetables there did not rise over the following three years.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy described above?
choices: Fruit and vegetables at Tolland's full-service grocery stores cost more, on average, than the same items do at corner shops.
People who care most about eating fresh produce tend to move to neighborhoods that already have full-service grocery stores.
Before the new stores opened, many residents of those neighborhoods said they would buy more produce if a store were nearby.
Residents of neighborhoods with full-service grocery stores also tend to eat less fast food than other Tolland residents typically do.
The new grocery stores are larger, on average, than the full-service stores in Tolland's other neighborhoods.
questions.explanation: If people who care about eating produce choose to live where stores already are, the first fact reflects who lives near stores, not what stores do to residents, so a new store need not change anyone's diet; that is B. A is tempting because it gives a reason residents might not buy produce at the new stores, but it leaves unexplained why residents near the existing stores eat more.

setup.label: Paradox
setup.text: People who live near full-service grocery stores eat more produce, but opening new stores didn't raise produce eating in the neighborhoods that got them.

breakdown.analysis: If stores make people eat more produce, new stores should have worked. They didn't. So maybe the store isn't the cause of the first pattern at all. Who lives near stores? Maybe the produce lovers moved there. That's a self-selection explanation, and it lets both facts be true. We need an answer that says the link in fact 1 comes from who chooses to live where, not from the store.

choices.note: Tempting, because it gives a reason the new stores might not change buying. But it explains only one side. If store produce is pricier, why do residents near the existing stores eat more? The first fact is left hanging.
CORRECT. Fact 1 then reflects who chooses to live near stores, not an effect of the stores. A new store doesn't change the diets of the people already living there, so fact 2 fits too.
This deepens the puzzle. Residents said they'd buy more, and then didn't.
So? Another difference between the groups doesn't explain why new stores changed nothing.
If anything, bigger stores should have helped more. This doesn't resolve anything.

questions.stimulus: Columnist: Last year the town of Haverly doubled its tax on commercial properties left vacant, hoping to push landlords to fill the empty storefronts on its main streets. This year, eleven of the town's thirty empty storefronts have found new tenants. The tax increase, then, has succeeded in reducing the number of empty storefronts in Haverly.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption on which the columnist's argument depends?
choices: Landlords in Haverly generally pay close attention to changes in local tax rates on commercial property.
The tax increase will continue to reduce the number of empty storefronts in Haverly in future years.
The doubled tax is higher than the tax on vacant commercial property in any neighboring town.
Not all of the eleven storefronts would have found new tenants this year had the vacancy tax not been increased.
None of the storefronts in Haverly that were occupied last year has become empty at any time since then.
questions.explanation: To credit the tax, the columnist must assume that at least some of the new leases would not have happened anyway; negate D (all eleven would have been filled regardless) and the tax accomplished nothing. E is the tempting too-strong trap: a few new vacancies would not sink the argument, so the argument does not need zero.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The tax increase has succeeded in reducing the number of empty storefronts.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: After the tax doubled, eleven of thirty empty storefronts found tenants.

breakdown.analysis: Eleven storefronts filled. Would they have filled anyway? Storefronts get rented every year. If all eleven would have been leased without the tax, the tax did nothing. A claim that a policy caused something needs the outcome not to have happened anyway. We need an answer that says at least some of those leases depended on the tax.

choices.note: Not required. Negate it: landlords don't generally watch tax rates. Some still could have, and the tax could still have worked.
choices.negation: Landlords in Haverly do not generally pay close attention to tax changes. (A few might, and the argument can survive.)

choices.note: Future years are beside the point. The conclusion is about what the tax has already done.
choices.negation: The tax will not keep reducing vacancies in future years. (Past success is untouched.)

choices.note: Irrelevant comparison. Haverly's tax could be lower than a neighbor's and still have worked.
choices.negation: Some neighboring town has a tax on vacant properties at least as high as Haverly's. (No effect on whether Haverly's tax worked.)

choices.note: CORRECT. Negate it: all eleven would have been filled anyway. Then the tax caused none of the drop, and the argument falls apart.
choices.negation: All eleven storefronts would have found tenants this year even without the tax increase.

choices.note: Tempting, because new vacancies could offset the eleven. But 'none' is too strong. Negated, one or two storefronts went empty, and the number of empty storefronts still fell.
choices.negation: At least one storefront that was occupied last year has become empty. (With eleven filled, the total can still drop.)

questions.stimulus: Last year, first-year students at Ostby College who used the campus writing center at least once passed the required composition course at a much higher rate than first-year students who never used it. So the college should require every first-year student to visit the writing center, since doing so will raise the proportion of first-year students who pass the composition course.
questions.stem: Which one of the following would be most useful to know in order to evaluate the argument?
choices: Whether students who chose to use the writing center were already stronger writers than those who did not
How much the college spends each year to pay the tutors who staff the writing center
How many of the college's first-year students enrolled in the required composition course last year
Whether the composition course is graded more strictly at Ostby than at other colleges in the region
Whether any students who passed the course last year also used the library's tutoring services
questions.explanation: Students chose whether to use the writing center, so the ones who did may already have been the stronger writers; A tells us whether the center or prior skill explains the gap. D is tempting because it is about how the course is graded, but every student being compared took the same Ostby course, so the answer cannot affect the comparison.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Requiring every first-year student to visit the writing center will raise the composition pass rate.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Last year, students who used the center passed at a much higher rate than those who didn't.

breakdown.analysis: Who goes to a writing center voluntarily? Maybe the motivated, already-capable students. If so, the center didn't make the difference; the students did, and forcing everyone to go won't copy the result. An evaluate answer should be a two-sided question: one answer helps the argument, the other hurts it. We need: were the users already better writers?

choices.note: CORRECT. Yes: the gap may be prior skill, and the requirement may do little. No: the center looks like the cause, and the plan looks good. Either answer moves the argument.
Wrong dimension. Cost doesn't tell us whether the requirement would raise pass rates.
The argument is about rates, not totals. The number enrolled doesn't affect whether users passed because of the center.
Tempting, since grading affects pass rates. But both groups took the same course at Ostby, so grading standards are the same on both sides of the comparison.
Too vague. 'Any' students using other help doesn't tell us whether one group used it more, so neither answer moves the argument.

questions.stimulus: Rail engineer: On the Calder line, broken rails are reported far more often in winter than in summer. Some attribute this to the heavier freight traffic that the line carries in winter. But the more likely cause is that cold makes the steel rails contract, putting them under tension that can open small flaws into breaks.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the rail engineer's argument?
choices: Freight traffic on the Calder line is heavier in winter than it is in any other season of the year.
Steel rails also expand in hot weather, and that expansion can cause them to buckle out of line.
Most of the Calder line's rails were installed more than thirty years ago and have never been replaced.
Winter rail breaks on the Calder line are most common on the stretches of track that carry the most freight.
Most winter breaks on the line occur just before dawn, when it is coldest and freight traffic is lightest.
questions.explanation: If breaks cluster in the coldest hours, when freight traffic is at its lightest, the timing fits the contraction mechanism and cuts against the traffic explanation, so E strengthens. B is the on-topic trap: it adds another effect of temperature on rails, but buckling in summer heat says nothing about why rails break in winter.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Winter rail breaks on the Calder line are more likely caused by cold contraction than by heavier freight traffic.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Breaks are far more common in winter; cold makes steel contract and puts rails under tension.

breakdown.analysis: Two suspects: cold and freight. Both are higher in winter, so seasonal data alone can't separate them. What could? Finer timing. If the mechanism is cold contraction, breaks should pile up when it's coldest. If it's freight, they should pile up when trains are heaviest. We need an answer that pulls those apart in the cold's favor.

choices.note: This supports the rival explanation. Heavier winter freight is exactly what the other side relies on. Wrong direction.
Tempting, since it shows temperature matters for rails. But it's about heat and buckling, not cold and breaks. It doesn't help decide between cold and freight in winter.
Irrelevant. Old rails could break from either cause; this doesn't favor one.
This points to freight. Breaks tracking freight volume weakens the engineer's claim.
CORRECT. Breaks cluster when it's coldest and freight is lightest. The timing matches the contraction mechanism and points away from traffic.

questions.stimulus: Runner: The organizers of the Ashby Marathon allowed two entrants who were injured in training to defer their paid entries to next year's race. I too was injured in training, as seriously as they were and at the same point before the race, yet my request to defer was refused. Since the organizers are obligated to treat entrants in the same situation alike, they must let me defer my entry as well.
questions.stem: The runner's argument is flawed because it
choices: presumes, without providing justification, that the two other entrants' injuries were as serious as the runner's own injury
draws a general conclusion about how all marathon organizers should behave from the conduct of one race's organizers
overlooks the possibility that the organizers could satisfy their obligation by revoking the deferrals granted to the other two entrants
takes for granted that the organizers refused the runner's request out of some personal dislike for the runner
fails to consider that the runner might be able to sell or transfer the entry to another runner instead
questions.explanation: Consistency can be restored either by granting the runner's deferral or by revoking the other two, so the duty to treat like cases alike doesn't show the organizers must say yes; (C) names that overlooked option. (A) is the dominant trap: it questions whether the cases are alike, but the runner states that as a premise, so it isn't a flaw in the reasoning. (E) points to an option that has nothing to do with what equal treatment requires.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The organizers must let the runner defer the entry.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Organizers must treat entrants in the same situation alike; two injured entrants were allowed to defer; the runner was injured just as seriously, at the same point, and was refused.

breakdown.analysis: Does treating like cases alike require saying yes to the runner? Not necessarily. Right now the organizers have treated three like entrants differently: two got a yes, one got a no. Consistency can be restored two ways: grant the runner a deferral too, or take back the other two. The runner assumes the only fix is the one the runner wants. It's like a child saying, 'You let my brother stay up late, so to be fair you have to let me stay up too.' A parent could be just as fair by sending the brother to bed. We need an answer that points to the other way of being consistent. Most students pick (A), because 'maybe their situations differ' is the standard objection to a fairness argument. But the runner states outright that the injuries were as serious and came at the same point. That's a premise, and the LSAT asks you to accept premises; a flaw answer has to describe the move from premises to conclusion.

choices.note: Tempting, because 'maybe the cases differ' is the usual way to attack a fairness argument. But the runner says outright that the injuries were equally serious; that's a premise, and you accept premises. The problem is what the runner concludes from them.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: My neighbor got a permit for a fence, so I should get one too (with nothing said about whether the two yards are alike).

choices.note: No generalization happens. The runner draws a conclusion only about this race's organizers and this one request.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: The Ashby organizers grant deferrals, so every marathon in the country should grant them.

choices.note: CORRECT. The obligation is to treat like entrants alike, not to treat them generously. Revoking the other two deferrals would satisfy it just as well as granting the runner's. So the obligation alone can't show the organizers must say yes.
The runner never says or needs anything about the organizers' motives. Whatever their reason for refusing, the argument stands or falls the same way.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: The organizers refused me only because they dislike me, so their refusal must be wrong.

choices.note: Tempting in a small way, because it also points to an option the runner ignores. But selling the entry has nothing to do with what equal treatment requires of the organizers, which is the only thing the conclusion rests on.

questions.stimulus: Election commissioner: A candidate for the Bramford town council should be exempted from the requirement to collect petition signatures if the candidate either currently holds an elected town office or has been nominated by a party that received at least 10 percent of the vote in the most recent council election, provided that the candidate has also filed a financial disclosure statement by the filing deadline.
questions.stem: Which one of the following judgments most closely conforms to the principle stated by the election commissioner?
choices: Okafor, nominated by a party that won 12 percent of the vote in the last council election, should be exempted, since that party's nominees always have been.
Brandt, nominated by a party that won 15 percent of the vote in the last council election, filed his disclosure before the deadline and should be exempted.
Varga, who filed his financial disclosure on time and who served on the town council until last year, should be exempted.
Haddad, who currently serves as town clerk, an elected town office, should be exempted, since she plans to file her disclosure next week.
Lindqvist, who holds no elected office and who filed her financial disclosure on time, should not be exempted, since no party has nominated her.
questions.explanation: An exemption is warranted when the candidate meets either the office or the party condition and has also filed disclosure by the deadline; Brandt meets the party condition and filed before the deadline, so B conforms. E is tempting, but the principle states only when a candidate should be exempted, not when one should be refused, so it cannot justify denying Lindqvist an exemption.

setup.label: Principle
setup.text: (Currently holds elected town office OR nominated by a party with 10%+ in the last council election) AND disclosure filed by deadline → should be exempted from petition signatures.

setup.label: Application
setup.text: Find the candidate who should be exempted and who meets every condition.

breakdown.analysis: The right answer must check three things: 1. a positive judgment (exempt), since the rule only says when to exempt; 2. either current elected office or a 10-percent party nomination; 3. disclosure filed by the deadline. Each trap leaves one of these unknown or unmet.

choices.note: The party condition is met, but we don't know whether Okafor filed the disclosure. Past practice isn't one of the conditions.
CORRECT. Party with 15 percent (meets the 10 percent condition), disclosure filed before the deadline, and a positive judgment. Every condition is satisfied.
Fails the office condition. Varga served until last year; the rule requires currently holding office. And no party nomination is mentioned.
The office condition is met, but disclosure is only planned for next week, and we don't know if that's before the deadline. Condition 3 is unknown.

Tempting, because Lindqvist does fail both the office and party conditions. But the rule tells you only when to exempt someone. It's silent about when to refuse, so it can't back a 'should not' judgment.

questions.stimulus: Every taxpayer in the province of Velm recently answered a survey about provincial taxes. Most of the respondents said that they believe they pay a larger share of their income in provincial taxes than most other Velm taxpayers do. Many respondents also said that provincial taxes are too high and that the burden is unfairly distributed.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is most strongly supported by the information above?
choices: Not every Velm taxpayer who believes that his or her provincial tax share is larger than most others' shares is correct.
Most Velm taxpayers are mistaken about how the share of their income that they pay in provincial taxes compares with others' shares.
Velm's provincial taxes place a heavier burden on most taxpayers than those taxpayers themselves believe.
Most Velm taxpayers pay a smaller share of their income in provincial taxes than they believe they pay.
The Velm taxpayers who pay the largest share of their income in provincial taxes are the most likely to call those taxes too high.
questions.explanation: It is impossible for most taxpayers to pay a larger share than most others, so some of those who believe they do must be wrong; (A) states this as 'not every taxpayer who believes it is correct.' (B) is the dominant trap: if, say, 60 percent hold the belief and about half really are above the middle, only around 10 percent need be mistaken, far short of most.

setup.label: Facts
setup.text: 1. Every Velm taxpayer answered; 2. most believe they pay a larger share of income in provincial taxes than most other Velm taxpayers; 3. many think taxes are too high and unfairly distributed.

breakdown.analysis: Can most people really pay more than most others? No. To pay more than most others, you have to be above the middle, and at most about half the people can be above the middle. So if more than half believe they're above the middle, some of them must be wrong. But only some. Imagine 100 taxpayers: 60 believe they're in the top half, and the top half really holds 50. At least 10 are wrong. Ten is not most. Watch the subset trap: 'some are mistaken' follows; 'most are mistaken' doesn't. Most students pick (B), because the belief is so widespread that it feels like most people must be wrong. The numbers above show they needn't be. The right answer hides as a double negative: 'not every believer is correct' is just 'some believers are wrong' in disguise. Most students pick (B), because the belief is so widespread that it feels like most people must be wrong. The numbers above show they needn't be. The right answer hides as a double negative: 'not every believer is correct' is just 'some believers are wrong' in disguise.

choices.note: CORRECT. 'Not every believer is correct' = 'at least one believer is wrong.' Since most believe they're above most others and at most about half can be, some believers must be wrong.
Tempting, and it's the classic trap. The numbers force only some mistakes, not most. With 60 believers and 50 real top-halfers, as few as 10 need be wrong.
Wrong direction and unsupported. If anything, the mistaken ones think their burden is relatively larger than it is.
Wrong dimension. The belief is about rank compared with others, not about the size of one's own share. Someone could know their own share exactly and simply underestimate everyone else's.
We don't know this. The stimulus never links actual tax share to opinions about whether taxes are too high.

questions.stimulus: Corlett's ordinance banning the use of leaf blowers before 8 a.m. exists solely to protect residents from early-morning noise. Battery-powered leaf blowers run almost silently, making less noise than an ordinary conversation. So the ordinance should not be applied to people using battery-powered blowers.
questions.stem: The pattern of reasoning in which one of the following is most similar to that in the argument above?
choices: The pool forbids glass containers on its deck because broken glass is very hard to see in water. Plastic containers cannot shatter. So the pool should require that all drinks sold on its deck be served in plastic.

The rule that hikers register before climbing Mount Feld is intended to help rescuers find lost hikers. In recent years rescuers have rarely needed to consult the register. So the rule should be abolished.

The museum forbids flash photography in its galleries because camera flashes can fade old pigments. Many visitors ignore the rule, especially in crowded rooms. So the museum should enforce the rule more strictly.

Holt Park's ban on campfires exists solely to prevent wildfires. Gas camp stoves with fully enclosed flames pose no risk of starting a wildfire. So the ban should not be enforced against campers using such stoves.

Our firm forbids personal phone calls during meetings because such calls distract the other attendees. A brief call is less distracting than a long one. So brief calls should be penalized less severely than long ones.
questions.explanation: The argument reasons that a rule's sole purpose does not apply to a certain kind of case, so the rule should not be applied to that case; D has the same structure with the campfire ban and enclosed stoves. B is tempting because it also reasons from a rule's purpose, but it concludes that the whole rule should be abolished, not that one kind of case should be exempt.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The early-morning leaf-blower ban should not be applied to battery-powered blowers.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The ban's only purpose is preventing early-morning noise; battery-powered blowers are nearly silent.

setup.label: Pattern
setup.text: Rule R exists only to prevent harm H; case C doesn't produce H; so R shouldn't be applied to C.

breakdown.analysis: Three parts to match: 1. a rule with a single stated purpose; 2. a kind of case that doesn't threaten that purpose; 3. the conclusion that the rule shouldn't apply to that kind of case (an exemption, not a new rule, not repeal). Check the conclusion of each choice first; that kills most of them fast.

choices.note: The conclusion is a new requirement (all drinks in plastic), not an exemption from the existing rule.
Tempting, because it reasons from the rule's purpose. But the conclusion is to abolish the rule for everyone, based on how rarely it's needed. The original exempts one kind of case.
Different direction: people break the rule, so enforce it harder. No case is shown to fall outside the rule's purpose.
CORRECT. Sole purpose: prevent wildfires. Enclosed stoves don't risk wildfires. So don't enforce the ban against them. Exact match.
The conclusion is about grading penalties, not about exempting a case. Brief calls still distract, just less.

questions.stimulus: Critic: The Halden Prize committee may consider a play only if that play premiered within the two years before the committee meets. Marrow Lane was first performed three years ago, in a workshop staging before a small invited audience; its first full professional production opened only last spring. Therefore, the committee may not consider Marrow Lane.
questions.stem: The conclusion of the critic's argument follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?
choices: Any play that premiered within the two years before the committee meets may then be considered by the committee.
A play need not have had a full professional production in order to be considered by the prize committee.
The committee may not consider any play that has been performed only in workshop stagings.
A play premieres no later than the first time it is performed before any audience, invited or not.
A workshop staging before an invited audience usually counts as the premiere of the play that is being staged.
questions.explanation: The rule makes a premiere within two years necessary, so the critic needs Marrow Lane's premiere to fall outside that window; (D) guarantees it, since the play was first performed three years ago and so premiered then or earlier. (E) is the dominant trap: it's the right idea, that the workshop was the premiere, but 'usually' doesn't guarantee it for Marrow Lane. (C) covers only plays performed solely in workshops.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The committee may not consider Marrow Lane.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Considered → premiered within the last two years; Marrow Lane was first performed (in a workshop) three years ago; its first full production opened last spring.

breakdown.analysis: When did Marrow Lane premiere: at the workshop three years ago, or at the full production last spring? The argument never says. Chain: Considered → premiered within 2 years. Contrapositive: NOT premiered within 2 years → NOT considered. So we need: Marrow Lane did NOT premiere within 2 years. The only way to get there is to tie 'premiere' to the first performance. If a play premieres no later than its first performance, Marrow Lane premiered three or more years ago → not within 2 years → not considered. Notice that the rule is a necessary condition; an answer that turns it into a sufficient one won't help. Most students pick (E), because it says just what the critic needs: the workshop counts as the premiere. But 'usually' leaves room for Marrow Lane to be an exception, and a sufficient assumption has to lock the conclusion in. Here the weak version of the right idea is the trap. Most students pick (E), because it says just what the critic needs: the workshop counts as the premiere. But 'usually' leaves room for Marrow Lane to be an exception, and a sufficient assumption has to lock the conclusion in. Here the weak version of the right idea is the trap.

choices.note: This reverses the rule. It tells us which plays may be considered, which can only help a play get in. It can't establish that Marrow Lane is excluded.
Tempting, because it hints the full production doesn't matter. But it doesn't say when Marrow Lane premiered, so we still can't tell whether it falls outside the window.
Tempting, because it targets workshops. But Marrow Lane had a full professional production too, so it wasn't performed 'only' in workshops. The rule doesn't reach it.

CORRECT. First performance was three years ago, so the premiere was then or earlier: outside the two-year window. Contrapositive of the rule: not considered. The conclusion is locked in. The awkward wording is typical of right answers.

Tempting. It's the right idea at the wrong strength. 'Usually' allows exceptions, and Marrow Lane could be one: maybe its premiere was the full production last spring. A sufficient assumption has to guarantee the conclusion, and this doesn't.

questions.stimulus: Psychologist: In a study of people beginning a twelve-week course of therapy, clients who were told at the outset that therapy often feels worse before it feels better were twice as likely to complete the full course as clients who were not told this. Yet among the clients who completed the course, those who had been told reported no greater improvement than those who had not. So telling clients what to expect does nothing to increase the number of clients who improve.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the psychologist's argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument
choices: takes for granted that clients who complete a full course of therapy improve more than do clients who drop out partway
treats a mere correlation between being told what to expect and completing therapy as proof that the one causes the other
fails to establish that the clients who were told what to expect actually understood what they were told
confuses the claim that being told what to expect is not sufficient for improvement with the claim that it is not necessary
overlooks the possibility that telling clients what to expect raises the number who improve by raising the number who finish
questions.explanation: The study shows that telling clients doubles completion and leaves improvement among completers unchanged; if completing therapy helps, telling clients raises the total number who improve simply by getting more of them to the end, which is the possibility (E) says the argument overlooks. (A) is the dominant trap because it names the key factor, but the argument does not assume that completers improve more; if anything, it needs the opposite.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Telling clients what to expect does nothing to increase the number of clients who improve.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Told clients were twice as likely to finish; among finishers, told and untold clients improved equally.

breakdown.analysis: Improvement per finisher was the same. Does that mean the number who improve is the same? No. Telling clients doubled the number who finished. If finishing therapy helps, then twice as many finishers means more improved people overall, even though each finisher improves the same amount. The psychologist compares people inside the finisher group and forgets that the size of that group changed. It's like saying a free-shuttle program doesn't increase concert attendance at the arena because each rider enjoys the show the same as people who drove; the point is that more people got there. We need an answer that says more completions can mean more improvement in total. Most students pick (A), because it names the key factor, whether finishers improve more. It fails because it's backwards: the argument doesn't assume that; it ignores that possibility. The right answer hides in an indirect route ('raises the number who improve by raising the number who finish') that's easy to dismiss on a first read. Most students pick (A), because it names the key factor, whether finishers improve more. It fails because it's backwards: the argument doesn't assume that; it ignores that possibility. The right answer hides in an indirect route ('raises the number who improve by raising the number who finish') that's easy to dismiss on a first read.

choices.note: Tempting, because it's about the exact factor that matters. But it's backwards. The argument doesn't assume finishers improve more; if they do, the argument fails. The flaw is ignoring that possibility, not assuming it.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Clients who finished improved, so finishing therapy must be what made them improve more than dropouts.

choices.note: The argument doesn't rely on this causal claim. Accepting that being told causes completion would actually work against its conclusion.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Told clients finished more often, so being told must be what made them finish.

choices.note: So? Whether they understood or not, the study measured the outcomes. This doesn't touch the gap between per-finisher improvement and total improvement.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Clients told about side effects had fewer complaints, so the warning worked (without checking they understood it).

choices.note: No conditional confusion. The argument never talks about what is necessary or sufficient for improvement.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Being told what to expect doesn't guarantee improvement, so clients can improve without being told.

choices.note: CORRECT. Same improvement per finisher, but twice as many finishers. If finishing helps, total improvement rises. The argument looks only inside the finisher group and ignores the change in its size.

questions.stimulus: Two seasons ago, the Mount Skelling ski area regraded its beginner slopes. Since then, the number of skiers treated by its first-aid staff for injuries suffered on those slopes has fallen from about two hundred a season to about one hundred thirty. So the regrading has made the beginner slopes a less dangerous place to ski.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the argument?
choices: The regraded beginner slopes cost the ski area considerably less to groom each night than the old slopes did.
Since the regrading, the ski school has taught most lessons for new skiers in a practice meadow beside the lodge.
Some skiers hurt on the beginner slopes go to a clinic in town instead of to the ski area's first-aid staff.
Skiers report that the regraded beginner slopes are more enjoyable to ski than the old slopes were.
The first-aid staff who treated injured skiers were the same people both before and after the regrading.
questions.explanation: The argument treats a drop in the number of injuries as a drop in danger, but if most new skiers now take their lessons in a meadow off the slopes, fewer people ski there and the count could fall with no change in risk (B). (C) is the dominant trap: some injured skiers bypassing first aid would undercount injuries, but nothing suggests that share changed after the regrading, so it can't explain the drop.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The regrading made the beginner slopes less dangerous.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Since the regrading, skiers treated by first aid for injuries on those slopes fell from about 200 a season to about 130.

breakdown.analysis: Is a lower injury count the same as a safer slope? Not if fewer people are skiing there. Danger is a rate (injuries per skier), and the argument gives only a count. If far fewer novices use the slopes, you'd expect fewer injuries even if the slopes are just as risky. It's like saying a road got safer because it had fewer crashes the year a bypass took most of its traffic. Watch the switch from a count to a rate. We need an answer that gives another reason the count fell, especially fewer (or fewer inexperienced) skiers on those slopes. Most students pick (C), because it attacks the measure: some injured skiers never reach first aid. But that was presumably true before the regrading too, so it can't explain a drop. A measurement problem weakens a before-and-after comparison only if it changed. The right answer hides: it's about where the ski school teaches, which looks irrelevant until you see it means far fewer novices on the beginner slopes.

choices.note: Irrelevant. Grooming costs are about money, not about how dangerous the slopes are.

CORRECT. If most new skiers now learn in a meadow instead of on the beginner slopes, far fewer people, and the least skilled ones, ski those slopes. Injuries would fall even if the slopes are no safer per skier. That's another explanation for the drop.

Tempting, because it says the first-aid count misses some injuries. But nothing says that changed with the regrading. If the same share went to the clinic before and after, the drop in the count is still real. A flawed measure weakens a before-and-after comparison only if the flaw changed.
If anything this strengthens: more enjoyable slopes would likely draw more skiers, which makes the drop in injuries more impressive, not less.
This strengthens the argument by ruling out a change in who recorded the injuries as the reason for the drop. Wrong direction.

questions.stimulus: Lionfish, an invasive predator on the Sollen Reef, eat large numbers of young reef fish. Last year the regional fisheries agency began paying divers a bounty for each lionfish they spear on the reef. Since then, divers have killed thousands of lionfish there, so the bounty program must be easing the pressure on the reef's young fish.
questions.stem: The argument depends on assuming which one of the following?
choices: Lionfish are the most important predator of young fish on the Sollen Reef, outranking all of its native predators.
Divers collecting the bounty do not spear any fish other than lionfish while they are diving on the reef.
The bounty program will eventually eliminate every lionfish from the Sollen Reef if it is continued.
Most of the lionfish killed by divers since the bounty began were adults rather than juveniles.
The lionfish that divers have killed have not all been replaced by newly arrived or newly hatched ones.
questions.explanation: Killing thousands of lionfish helps young reef fish only if the lionfish population actually ends up smaller, so the argument requires E. Negate it (the dead fish were all replaced) and predation is unchanged. D is tempting because big adults eat more, but killing juveniles also removes predators, so the argument doesn't need it.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The bounty program must be easing predation pressure on the reef's young fish.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Lionfish eat many young reef fish; divers have killed thousands of lionfish since the bounty began.

breakdown.analysis: Thousands killed. So what if thousands more showed up? Invasive species often bounce back fast. If new lionfish moved in or hatched as quickly as divers removed them, the reef has as many lionfish as before, and the young fish are no better off. We need an answer that says the kills weren't fully offset.

choices.note: Too strong. Lionfish can be the second-biggest predator and removing them still eases pressure.
choices.negation: Lionfish are not the most important predator of young fish on the reef. (Removing them can still help.)

choices.note: Too strong. A diver spearing the occasional grouper doesn't undo the benefit of thousands of dead lionfish.
choices.negation: Some divers spear at least one other kind of fish. (Pressure from lionfish can still be eased.)

choices.note: Too strong, and about the future. Easing pressure doesn't require total elimination.
choices.negation: The program will not eliminate lionfish from the reef. (Fewer lionfish can still mean less pressure.)

choices.note: Tempting, since big adults eat more. But juveniles eat young fish too, and killing them prevents future predators. Negated, the argument survives.
choices.negation: Most of the lionfish killed were juveniles. (Killing them still removes predators.)

choices.note: CORRECT. Negate it: every dead lionfish was replaced. Then the reef holds just as many predators, and the pressure hasn't eased. The argument collapses.
choices.negation: Every lionfish killed has been replaced by a newly arrived or newly hatched lionfish.

questions.stimulus: Last year, none of Dalvey County's steel bridges that had been treated with the new anticorrosion coating developed any rust. This year, every steel bridge in the county has been treated with that coating. So none of the county's steel bridges will develop rust this year.
questions.stem: Which one of the following arguments exhibits a flawed pattern of reasoning most similar to that exhibited by the argument above?
choices: Last year, every bakery in Dorne that won the city's pastry prize used imported butter. This year, every bakery in Dorne uses imported butter. So every bakery in Dorne will win the pastry prize this year.

Last spring, none of the hiking club's members who carried maps got lost. This spring, several members of the club plan to hike without maps. So several members of the hiking club will get lost this spring.
Every bus on the Route 4 line is inspected monthly, and no bus that is inspected monthly has ever broken down on its route. So no bus on the Route 4 line has ever broken down on its route.

Everyone who failed last year's chemistry final at Hale Academy had skipped the review sessions. This year, every chemistry student at Hale has attended them. So no chemistry student at Hale will fail this year's final.

None of the restaurants on Quay Street that were inspected last month had any health violations. Since those restaurants were chosen at random, probably few restaurants on Quay Street have any health violations.
questions.explanation: The argument takes a pattern seen in last year's treated bridges and treats it as guaranteed for a new, larger group; D does the same, phrased in contrapositive form (every student who failed skipped = no one who attended failed). A is tempting because its wording tracks the original closely, but it reverses the conditional, inferring the prize from the butter.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: None of the county's steel bridges will develop rust this year.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Last year no treated bridge rusted; this year every bridge is treated.

setup.label: Pattern
setup.text: Last time, no X had Y; now every member of a larger group is X; so none of them will have Y.

breakdown.analysis: What's wrong? Last year's treated bridges may have been the newest ones, or last year may have been dry. A pattern in one small group doesn't guarantee the same result for everyone later. So the match needs: past group with feature X had no Y → now all are X → so none will have Y. Watch the hard version: the right answer may state the past fact in contrapositive form. 'Everyone who failed had skipped' means the same thing as 'no one who attended failed.' Also watch for a choice that copies the wording but flips the conditional. Most students pick (A), because its wording tracks the original almost word for word. It fails because it reverses the conditional, inferring the prize from the butter. Most students pick (A), because its wording tracks the original almost word for word. It fails because it reverses the conditional, inferring the prize from the butter.

choices.note: Tempting, because it looks almost word-for-word like the original. But the conditional runs the other way: winners → butter. The conclusion infers winning from butter. That's a reversal, a different flaw.
Different flaw. This negates the condition (no map → lost) instead of extending the pattern to a new group.
This is valid, and it doesn't project a past pattern onto the future. Valid arguments can't match a flawed one.
CORRECT. 'Everyone who failed had skipped' = 'no one who attended failed.' Now everyone attends, so supposedly no one fails. Same leap from a past group to a guaranteed future result.
Different structure. It's a probabilistic generalization from a random sample, and a fairly reasonable one, not a guarantee projected onto a new group.
